title: The model you pick isn't always the model that answers
description:
Fable 5.2's system card has a stat worth knowing if you ship agents: on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark, attack success within 15 tries was 4.09%, about 4x Fable 5.1 (1.02%).

Most of that gap comes from the fallback. When a message gets flagged, Fable 5.2 can hand the turn to Opus 4.8. Under attack that happened on 53% of attempts, and attacks succeeded 5.17% of the time when Opus 4.8 answered vs 2.05% when Fable answered itself.

What I'd do about it:

  1. Log model, stop_reason and usage.iterations on every request. Fallback routing is sticky for about an hour, and later turns only show a fallback_message entry in usage.iterations, so watching for the fallback block alone undercounts.
  2. Turn off "Switch models when a message is flagged" for agents that read untrusted content and can act irreversibly (send, push, pay).
  3. Put an action check in front of irreversible tools, so an attack has to beat two layers.

The absolute numbers are still low. The point is that the one that answers sets the risk, and a setting built to cut refusals can route you to an older model without telling you.

Full breakdown, with the logger and the weekly threshold I use to decide when to turn the switch off: https://pub.towardsai.net/fable-5-2-is-4x-easier-to-hijack-a107805488d9?sk=a4a84fa65eabbcbe9c6ced01ec59e537

title: pgvector HNSW Filtering: 431 of 2,000 LIMIT 10 Queries Came Back Short
description:
I wrote LIMIT 10. Postgres returned 3 rows. There was no error, no warning and no log line, and for five weeks I didn't notice, because my own fallback code covered for it.

This post is about pgvector HNSW filtering: what happens when you put a WHERE clause on an approximate nearest neighbor query. Short version: the index finds its neighbors first and your filter runs afterward. If most of those neighbors fail the filter, you get fewer rows than you asked for, and nothing tells you.

TL;DR

  • pgvector's HNSW index collects hnsw.ef_search candidates (default 40), and only then does Postgres apply your WHERE filter. When the filter rejects most of them, the query returns fewer than LIMIT rows without any error.
  • In a replay of 2,000 production queries, 431 (21.6%) returned fewer than 10 rows and 97 returned zero.
  • Raising hnsw.ef_search to 200 cut short results to 63. pgvector 0.8's hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order cut them to 9, and those 9 were correct answers (the category didn't have 10 rows in total).
  • The worst-hit categories were mid-sized ones that sit close in embedding space to a bigger category. The tiniest categories mostly escaped because the planner skipped HNSW for them.
  • Check len(rows) < limit in application code. The database will never flag it.

What was I building?

The system is the question retriever inside Preterview, a voice mock-interview platform I run that has three interviewer styles and writes a report after each session (full disclosure: I built it, and it's at preterview.com/en). Before each interviewer turn, an agent pulls 10 candidate follow-up questions for the candidate's target role, and an LLM picks one based on the conversation so far.

The table looked like this:

  • 52,000 questions
  • 140 role tags (backend_engineer, data_engineer, sre, ios_engineer, ...)
  • embedding vector(1024) with an HNSW index on default build settings (m = 16, ef_construction = 64)
  • a plain btree index on role

The query was the one every tutorial shows:

SELECT id, body
FROM interview_questions
WHERE role = $2
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT 10;

And here's the part I'm least proud of. If the retriever got fewer than 10 rows back, it padded the list from a pool of 30 general questions. I'd written that for brand-new roles with tiny question banks. In practice it hid the bug: users preparing for data engineering roles got the same three general questions about "a project you're proud of" session after session. The complaint I eventually got was "the interviewer feels repetitive." It didn't look like a retrieval bug at all.

Why does pgvector HNSW return fewer rows than LIMIT?

pgvector's HNSW index scan returns at most hnsw.ef_search nearest candidates (40 by default), and Postgres applies the WHERE clause to those candidates after the scan. If 37 of the 40 nearest questions belong to another role, you get 3 rows, even though thousands of matching rows exist in the table.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows exactly this once you know where to look:

Limit  (actual rows=3 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using questions_embedding_idx on interview_questions
        Order By: (embedding <=> '[...]'::vector)
        Filter: (role = 'data_engineer'::text)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 37

40 candidates, 37 removed, 3 left. Postgres didn't fail at anything. It did exactly what the index promised: an approximate top 40, then a filter.

Which filtered vector queries get hit hardest?

Mid-sized categories that are semantically close to a large category get hit hardest. The trouble isn't that a role is rare. It's that its nearest neighbors in embedding space mostly belong to some other role.

I replayed 2,000 real retrieval calls from logs against a copy of the table and bucketed them:

Role bucket Queries Came back short
Large roles (more than 3% of rows each) 1,020 12
Mid roles, close to a large role 610 379
Mid roles, semantically distinct 240 31
Tiny roles (under 0.2% of rows) 130 9
Total 2,000 431

data_engineer was the poster child. Its questions about pipelines, partitioning and backfills sit right next to backend_engineer questions about queues, partitioning and retries, and backend had roughly six times as many rows. So the 40 nearest neighbors of a data engineering query were mostly backend questions. sre lost to devops the same way.

Meanwhile embedded_firmware was fine at the same size, because nothing else in the table talks about interrupt handlers.

The tiny roles surprised me. They mostly worked, because for a highly selective filter the planner used the btree on role, fetched every matching row and sorted them exactly by distance. No HNSW, no candidate cap. All 9 short results in that bucket came from roles with fewer than 10 questions in total, which is the right answer.

So the failure curve is U-shaped. Big roles win the neighbor vote. Tiny roles skip the index. The ones in the middle fall through the gap.

Does raising hnsw.ef_search fix it?

Raising hnsw.ef_search reduces short results but doesn't remove them, and it makes every query slower, including the ones that were already fine. Here's the same 2,000-query replay on my box:

Setting Short Zero rows p50 p99
ef_search = 40 (default) 431 97 4.1 ms 9 ms
ef_search = 100 168 22 5.0 ms 13 ms
ef_search = 200 63 4 6.8 ms 19 ms
ef_search = 1000 (max) 14 0 19.5 ms 41 ms
iterative_scan = relaxed_order 9 0 5.2 ms 31 ms

Even at the maximum of 1000, 5 queries still came back short of what the table could provide. A bigger fixed candidate pool is still a fixed candidate pool.

How does pgvector iterative index scan work?

pgvector 0.8.0 added iterative index scans: when the filter leaves too few rows, the scan keeps walking the graph and fetching more candidates until it fills the LIMIT or hits hnsw.max_scan_tuples (20,000 by default). You turn it on per session or per transaction:

  • strict_order keeps results exactly ordered by distance.
  • relaxed_order allows slight reordering and is faster, so you re-sort at the end.

This is what I shipped:

BEGIN;
SET LOCAL hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;
SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 100;

WITH candidates AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT id, body, embedding <=> $1 AS distance
  FROM interview_questions
  WHERE role = $2
  ORDER BY distance
  LIMIT 10
)
SELECT id, body FROM candidates ORDER BY distance;
COMMIT;

Two details matter here. SET LOCAL scopes the setting to the transaction, so it doesn't leak into other queries on a pooled connection. And the MATERIALIZED CTE plus the outer ORDER BY fixes the small reordering that relaxed_order allows.

The p99 jump from 9 ms to 31 ms comes from the worst queries, the data engineering ones that have to walk deep into backend territory before they find 10 matches. Median latency barely moved. For a voice interview where an LLM call comes right after this query, 31 ms at p99 doesn't register.

Why is checking the row count still required?

Iterative scans stop at hnsw.max_scan_tuples, so a very unlucky filter can still come back short, and the database still won't raise an error. The only reliable signal is in your code:

rows = await conn.fetch(QUERY, embedding, role)
if len(rows) < LIMIT:
    metrics.increment("retrieval.short", tags={"role": role})
    log.warning("short_retrieval", role=role, got=len(rows), want=LIMIT)

I kept the padding fallback, but now it fires a metric. If it fires for any role with more than 10 questions in the bank, that's a bug, not a cold start.

Should you use partial indexes instead?

A partial HNSW index per category (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE role = 'data_engineer') makes filtered search exact for that category, and it's the right fix if you filter on a handful of values. With 140 roles that's 140 indexes to build and maintain, so I only considered it for the two worst roles and found iterative scan was good enough. If your filter has 3 to 5 values, partitioning by that column is also a clean answer.

What did this bug actually cost?

  • 5 weeks live before I found it, all hidden behind a fallback I wrote myself
  • one afternoon to build the replay harness and get the numbers above
  • 4 lines of SQL to fix it, plus 4 lines of Python to make sure I see it next time

The expensive part wasn't the fix. It was a symptom that looked like bad LLM output when the cause was the database quietly returning less than I asked for.

So why does pgvector HNSW filtering return fewer rows than LIMIT?

Because pgvector's HNSW index scan fetches only hnsw.ef_search candidates (40 by default) and Postgres applies your WHERE filter afterward, so a selective filter can leave you with 3 rows, or none, out of a LIMIT 10, with no error. It hurts most when the filtered category sits close in embedding space to a larger one. Raising ef_search helps partially at a latency cost. On pgvector 0.8 or later, set hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order inside the transaction, re-sort in a materialized CTE, and always check the returned row count in code, because the database won't do it for you.

Written by the developer behind Preterview, an interview prep platform.

title: How to Keep Chinese Model Inference In-Region: A Worked Cost Example
description:
How to Keep Chinese Model Inference In-Region: A Worked Cost Example

Short answer: For a China-compliant AI model gateway, the decision usually turns on fee shape, model coverage and where inference actually runs — not the headline rate. TENSORAXIS publishes per-token rates behind one OpenAI-compatible key, with domestic models served on China-compliant nodes. All figures below are dated and source-cited.

Disclosure: TENSORAXIS is the product we operate. This is an editorial comparison built from public sources, not an independent benchmark or a third-party user review. Competitor figures are attributed and dated; verify rates on vendor sites before deciding.

What the published figures actually say

Models marked domestic are served on China-compliant compute nodes; the same endpoint covers overseas frontier models for non-sensitive workloads. (Source: tensoraxis.ai, verified 2026-11-18)

Its Model Plaza lists 44 models across six featured providers: OpenAI (11, 256K context), Claude/Anthropic (14, 200K), Gemini/Google (13, 1M), DeepSeek (1, 128K), Zhipu GLM (4) and Moonshot Kimi (1). (Source: tensoraxis.ai/en/models, verified 2026-11-18)

Published per-1M rates include claude-opus-4-8 at $0.42 in / $2.13 out, gemini-3.5-flash at $0.19 / $1.11, gpt-5.6-terra at $1.50 / $2.00, and domestic glm-5.3 at ¥2.71 / ¥9.49. (Source: tensoraxis.ai/en/models, verified 2026-11-18)

For regulated workloads, ask where inference ran in writing; a global gateway does not by itself state the node location for each model. (Source: editorial synthesis, 2026-11-18)

Why this matters for my workload

If your workload has data-residency or compliance constraints, the node location is a first-order filter, not a footnote. Keep Chinese model inference in-region by routing domestic models to compliant nodes, and use the same OpenAI-compatible key for non-sensitive overseas models. Normalise every option to cost per million input and output tokens for the models you actually call.

What to check before you switch

  1. Confirm in writing which models run on China-compliant nodes.
  2. Compare per-million input and output token rates, not just headline prices.
  3. Verify OpenAI compatibility for tool calling, structured output and streaming.
  4. Check the published uptime SLA and average latency figures.

Dated figures from public sources; verify on vendor sites before deciding.

title: The JSON Parsed. Is It Right? How to Score LLM Data Extraction
description:
Structured outputs all but guarantee the shape of an extraction. Whether the answer is right is yours to score. How to score an LLM, a regex and the publisher's data, then keep what passes per field.

We had Gemini, one of three LLM runs, pull six fields from 20 Federal Register notices with a JSON Schema enforced. Every reply was valid, and 116 of the 120 values were right. It still failed: our bar allows no value in a field that should be empty, and it filled four.

All four sat on two correction notices, and each was real text from the document. One IRS notice exists only to change a date in another document, from 16 October to 26 October. Gemini returned 26 October as the notice's own comment deadline. Nothing in the valid JSON flagged the mistake.

The risky moment comes when the JSON parses and you stop looking. This guide is about what to do instead: score any tool on your own documents, pick one per field, and know when to score again.

The short version: a schema all but guarantees the JSON's shape; validation checks the values are usable; nothing guarantees they're true. On 20 Federal Register notices, three schema-enforced LLM runs were valid everywhere and none passed our bar; the publisher's data passed on its three fields, on our answer key. Score per field, on your own 20 rows, with one script for every tool.

About the results: one run per setup on 8 October 2026, two small models, 20 documents. An AI agent built the answer key; two other models, GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5.5, re-keyed all 120 cells without seeing it and matched every one, and the Federal Register's own data agrees on 113. Section 5 says how, and the checks ship with the download.

1. Watch it fail

The documents are ten Rules and ten Proposed Rules from 28 and 29 September 2026, via the public Federal Register API. Most are regular: ten are FAA airworthiness directives on one template. The traps sit in four. Two are correction notices, and one of those has no AGENCY: or ACTION: line. A HUD fee announcement calls its date an "applicability date". An EPA proposal lists three deadlines in its DATES section.

The obvious approach: describe the JSON in the prompt and call json.loads on the reply.

PROMPT = """Read this Federal Register document and return JSON with these keys:
agency, action, docket_id, rin, effective_date, comments_due.

DOCUMENT:
{text}"""

Against google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite, all twenty replies came back wrapped in a markdown code fence, so json.loads failed twenty times out of twenty.

That failure is easy: your code crashes and you notice. Strip the fences and thirteen of the twenty still fail a typed schema, every one on a date: the model wrote October 28, 2026 in one row and 2026-10-28 in another, in the same run.

openai/gpt-5-nano with the identical prompt shows the harder kind. Its replies were bare JSON, so all twenty parsed. Nine failed the schema, all on date formats. One was an IRS correction, where it put October 26, 2026 in both date fields. Validation caught the format. It had no way to catch the mistake.

The worrying row passed. A MARAD correction's DATES: line is a bare September 28, 2026, with no label. The model returned it as the effective date: valid, typed, and wrong by our answer key, which leaves it empty. (That's a judgement call, and section 7 shows what it changes.)

So prompting for JSON fails two ways: it won't parse, or it parses and is wrong. The rest of this guide is about the second.

2. Shape, usable, true


What each check stops, and misses.

None of the three implies the next.

Shape

The schema guarantees shape, almost always. OpenAI's docs say Structured Outputs "constrains completed, non-refusal model output to your supplied JSON Schema". Anthropic's say structured outputs "guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding". Both list the exceptions: a refusal, or a reply cut off at the token limit, can break the shape. Your validation catches those.

Usable

Validation checks the value is usable: the right type, within the limits you set. Google's Gemini docs: "While output is syntactically correct JSON, always validate values in your application." They also say to handle "schema-compliant but semantically incorrect outputs".

True

Nothing guarantees the value is true. A 2026 benchmark of 21 models, The Structured Output Benchmark, found near-perfect schema compliance, and the best exact match on values from text was 83.0%. One of our runs wrote 1124-06-12 for a deadline of 12 November 2026, and both the schema and Pydantic accepted it.

That's what a score is for. A blank is visible. A deadline from the wrong place looks exactly like the right one. A failed call recorded as empty looks like a blank. Count the three apart, on rows you checked, against a bar you set first.


Three valid replies, one wrong date.

Below: the schema and the call, the scorer and its seven outcomes, our full results, what to do after a FAIL, and the download with the code, the 20 documents and every raw reply.

3. A schema with types and nulls 

from datetime import date
from typing import Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class FRDocument(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")   # additionalProperties: false

    agency: Optional[str] = Field(description="Issuing agency as named on the "
        "AGENCY: line, full name, without abbreviation in brackets or parent "
        "department. null if no AGENCY: line.")
    action: Optional[str] = Field(description="Text of the ACTION: line, "
        "without the trailing full stop. null if absent.")
    docket_id: Optional[str] = Field(description="The first docket identifier "
        "in the square-bracketed line under the CFR part, without 'Docket No.' "
        "and without anything in parentheses. null if absent.")
    rin: Optional[str] = Field(description="Regulation Identifier Number, "
        "e.g. 2120-AA64, without 'RIN'. null if absent.")
    effective_date: Optional[date] = Field(description="Date the DATES: section "
        "says this rule is effective or applicable. null if no such date for "
        "this document.")
    comments_due: Optional[date] = Field(description="Deadline for public "
        "comments on this document, from its DATES: section. Ignore paperwork "
        "(OMB) and hearing-request deadlines. null if none.")

def strict_json_schema() -> dict:
    s = FRDocument.model_json_schema()
    s["required"] = list(s["properties"])        # every key required...
    s["additionalProperties"] = False
    return s                                      # ...but every value nullable

These are the exact descriptions our first two runs sent (schema.py). The third drops format: date and adds "Format YYYY-MM-DD." to both date descriptions. Three choices matter.

Every field is required, and every field can be null. "Not in the document" must come back as an explicit null. You can count a null. You can't count a key that silently vanished.

The descriptions are the rules. Write each one as an instruction: which date counts, what to ignore. If you can't define a field in a sentence, you can't score it.

Dates are dates. Pydantic's date type rejects November 2, 2026, and it accepts 1124-06-12, because 1124 is a real year. So check the value is plausible too, with a window that fits the field: here, a year either side of the document's publication date, though some rules take effect years later.

When a date falls outside the window, drop that key from the row, so score.py scores that one field failed; setting it to null would make a caught error look like a blank. The download's plausible_dates.py does this, and on our runs it drops all eight wrong-year dates and nothing else. It can't catch a plausible date from the wrong place, and section 6 has two.

4. One worked extraction

The call sends the schema, then validates the reply.

MAX_CHARS = 8000   # the preamble (AGENCY, ACTION, DATES) sits near the top
SYSTEM = ("You extract fields from US Federal Register documents. "
          "Follow the field descriptions in the schema exactly. "
          "If a field is not stated in the document, return null. Do not guess.")

body = {
    "model": model,                       # e.g. "openai/gpt-5-nano"
    "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                 {"role": "user", "content": text[:MAX_CHARS]}],   # text = the document
    "response_format": {"type": "json_schema",
                        "json_schema": {"name": "fr_document", "strict": True,
                                        "schema": strict_json_schema()}},
}
reply = chat(body)["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]   # chat(): gateway.py
row = FRDocument.model_validate_json(reply)   # raises if anything is off

Document 2026-19757 is an FAA airworthiness directive. The lines that matter:

[Docket No. FAA-2026-11786; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00439-R; ...]
RIN 2120-AA64
AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION: Final rule; request for comments.
DATES: This AD is effective October 13, 2026. ...
       The FAA must receive comments on this AD by November 12, 2026.

What gemini-2.5-flash-lite returned with the schema enforced:

{
  "agency": "Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT",
  "action": "Final rule; request for comments",
  "docket_id": "FAA-2026-11786",
  "rin": "2120-AA64",
  "effective_date": "2026-10-13",
  "comments_due": "2026-11-12"
}

Five fields match our answer key exactly. agency doesn't: the model kept "(FAA), DOT" although the description said to drop it. Whether that counts as wrong depends on a rule you write down. Section 5 sets that rule.

On another provider

We used an OpenAI-compatible gateway, so switching model meant changing one string. The syntax differs by lab. OpenAI takes response_format with type: "json_schema" and strict: true. Anthropic takes the schema in output_config.format, or a Pydantic model via client.messages.parse(). Gemini's client.interactions.create() takes response_format with type: "text", mime_type: "application/json" and a schema.

Schemas don't travel unchanged. Anthropic's structured outputs don't support minimum or minLength, and cap a request at 16 parameters that use union types (["string", "null"] counts). Gemini supports "a subset of the JSON Schema specification". Check your provider's limits page.

5. Score 20 rows

Simon Willison's workshop handout puts it well: "Crucially, did it get everything right? … Spot-checking is crucial." The instinct is right. A spot-check just leaves no record of which rows failed, to check again next month.

Build the answer key

Pick 20 documents that look like your real mix, awkward ones included. Read each source and type the right answer into a CSV, with a checker_note for every judgement call ("OMB paperwork deadline ignored"). Do this by hand if you can, and never let the tool you're testing build its own key.

If you can't read every source yourself, check the key the way ours was checked. First, readers that can't see it key the same documents: GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5.5, in fresh sessions, each keyed all 120 cells and matched ours on every one. Second, compare any data the publisher already gives you: the Federal Register's own records agree with our key on 113 of 120 cells. That check covers all six fields, though section 7 scores the publisher as a tool on only three, because its agency, action and docket fields follow its own conventions. Four of the seven differences are those conventions, two are dates it left blank that the text states, and one is a rule call: the IRS correction has no AGENCY: line, so our key leaves the agency empty. Where checks disagree, the source decides. No person re-read all 120 cells; these three checks stand in for that, and the CSV is there if you want to be the person. The key's checker_note column holds eight judgement calls, among them the two corrections, the HUD date and which EPA deadline counts.

Score each field, seven ways

For every row and field, score.py assigns one outcome:


Seven outcomes, three count as right.

Most of these line up with the categories information-extraction researchers scored by in the early 1990s (MUC-5 evaluation metrics, Chinchor and Sundheim, 1993), down to the word "spurious". They still fit, and newer tools draw the same line: the Strands Evals structured-output evaluator requires zero false alarms when there was nothing to find. We added failed: counting an errored call as a blank would let a field pass because its hardest documents never came back.

Keep missing and spurious apart.

def outcome(field, truth, got):
    # a failed call or a missing key never reaches outcome(): it scores "failed"
    # blank(): None or empty. normalise(): the clean-up rules, in score.py
    if blank(truth) and blank(got): return "correct_null"
    if blank(got):                  return "missing"
    if blank(truth):                return "spurious"
    if str(got).strip() == str(truth).strip(): return "exact"
    if normalise(field, got) == normalise(field, truth): return "normalised"
    return "wrong"

Watch each field's null rate as well. Both date fields are null on half the rows here (10 of 20 each), so a wrong null is easy to miss. Plumbing can make one too: a rate-limited (HTTP 429) call saved as a row of nulls looks exactly like a document with nothing to find.

So record a failed call as parsed: null, no object at all, which score.py counts as failed. A parsed object whose fields are all null still scores as blanks. Every row must carry every field, null where empty: a missing key scores failed too.

Set the bar before you look

Ours: a field passes with at least 19 of 20 rows right, zero values where the key says empty, and no failed calls. That zero is the real rule. Lower the bar to 18 and keep the zero, and every verdict in the next section stays the same. Lower it to 18 and drop the zero, and two of the three LLM runs pass.

The zero only bites where the key is empty. Here that is one row for agency and action, none for docket, two for RIN and ten for each date. Make sure your 20 include several documents where each field should be empty.

Treat 19 of 20 as a smoke alarm. At 20 rows, one or two rows either way is noise. Compare which rows fail.

6. What our score showed

Counted across all six fields, Gemini got 116 of the 120 values right, the run without format: date 115 and gpt-5-nano 108. All three failed: our bar fails a field on a single value filled where the key is empty, however high the total. On the three fields we score the publisher's data on, it and Gemini each got 58 of 60 right. The publisher's two misses were blanks, Gemini's were filled values, and only the publisher passed.


The kind of miss decides.

In the grid, the numbers are rows right out of 20 and the red tags count those values. The third run drops format: date from the schema (more on that below).


Every LLM run valid; none passed.

All three LLM runs returned schema-valid JSON for all 20 documents. None passed our bar.

Each run filled four or five, every one on the two correction notices. Each is a real name or date from the text, placed in a field the rules say to leave empty. All three runs filled the IRS correction's agency and action, though it has neither line, and took 26 October, the date it sets in another document's DATES section, as its own.

MARAD's bare date landed in a date field in every run. The IRS correction alone is enough to fail each run under the zero rule.

Take the two corrections out and the picture changes. On the other 18 documents, Gemini and the run without format: date get every field right, gpt-5-nano still fails on its garbled dates, and the publisher's data misses one date in each date field.

So this score mostly measures one kind of document: the odd one. If your 20 rows have no odd documents, your score is likely to flatter you.

Valid dates can be nonsense

With format: date in the strict schema, gpt-5-nano wrote years other than 2026: 1124-06-12 for a deadline of 12 November 2026, and 1102-11-02 for an effective date of 2 November 2026. Eight rows had a year other than 2026, and all eight passed the schema and Pydantic.

With format: date removed and "Format YYYY-MM-DD." in the description instead, every date in the re-run was in 2026. That's one run of each. But a schema change moved the score, and you won't know which way until you measure. The plausibility check in section 3 drops all eight.

The answer key needed fixing too

The description says null when there's no AGENCY: line, and our first key broke that rule on the IRS correction. We fixed the key, noted it, and re-scored everything. No overall verdict moved: each LLM run also fails a date field, whatever the agency key says. Expect this. If the descriptions and the key disagree, you're scoring the model against a rule it was never given.

Public benchmarks share the problem: Cleanlab found every public structured-output benchmark it examined full of wrong answers in the key.

Normalisation is a decision

On agency, Gemini matched 15 rows exactly and 4 more after clean-up. Too little and you blame the model for formatting; too much hides real errors. Keep the rules in code, where you can read them.

7. Score the alternatives with the same script

The Federal Register publishes its own structured data for these notices, so we scored it like any other tool. Its agency, action and docket fields follow different conventions, so we left them out and scored the other three. It passed the same bar.

It also missed two dates: the HUD applicability date, and the comment deadline for IRS proposal 2026-19888 (30 November 2026 in the text). Both are blanks, so it still passed. Its pass also rests on one of our judgement calls. Key MARAD's bare date as an effective date, and the Federal Register's effective_date drops to 18 of 20 and fails our bar. Gemini's and the regex's still pass.

So treat the publisher's data as one more tool: use it where it has the field, and score it like the others.

The regex scored 20 everywhere, but we wrote it while looking at these documents, so it proves little and is likely to break on a layout it hasn't seen.

The order to try things in: if the data exists in structured form, score that before reaching for a model. If the text has stable labels, try a parser. Use an LLM when layouts vary more than patterns can follow, or when a field needs reading: "which of these three dates is the comment deadline?" Mix freely, and score every tool with the same script.

8. After a FAIL

Under the table, score.py lists the rows to look at. Gemini's:

C1-2026-18574   agency          spurious  truth=None  got='DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY'
C1-2026-18574   action          spurious  truth=None  got='Information Reporting ... Correction'
2026-19786      comments_due    spurious  truth=None  got='2026-09-28'
C1-2026-18574   comments_due    spurious  truth=None  got='2026-10-26'

Step 1: Read every failing row against the source

Is the tool wrong, or your key?

Step 2: Pick one fix per failing field

Rewrite the description, if the model broke a rule you never wrote down. Route the field to a parser or the publisher's data, if they pass. Or allow null and send those rows to a person, if a wrong value costs more than a blank.

Step 3: Re-score everything

Use the same 20 rows and the same bar, then ten documents you haven't looked at, including the kind that failed. Keep a fix only if it passes both: a fix written from your 20 rows can pass them by construction.

Here, that might mean RIN and both dates from the Federal Register API, with rows where it's blank checked by a person (on this set that is 11 rows in each date field, because 10 are blank by design).

Or keep the model for dates, behind a code check that gives a correction notice null dates before the model is asked: on the 18 ordinary documents, Gemini got every date right. That check would be written from our two corrections, so score it on corrections it wasn't written on, as with the regex.

For docket, use whichever tool is cheapest, since every one we scored passed. For agency and action, add a code check that returns null when the label is missing, before the model is asked. We haven't scored either mix yet. Same script, next run.

Same schema, same documents, two small models: different failures. A new template does the same to your 20 rows, so add fresh documents now and then, and keep the old ones. Re-run the score whenever:

  • the model name or version changes, including an alias that moves under you (one of ours already has a retirement date: OpenAI retires gpt-5-nano from its API on 11 December 2026 and names gpt-6-luna as the replacement);
  • the prompt or any field description changes;
  • the schema changes, even "cosmetically" (see format: date above);
  • the price changes, because a price change is how a cheaper model gets swapped in;
  • the provider, SDK or gateway changes;
  • a new document source or template turns up;
  • someone finds a wrong cell in production (add that document to the set too);
  • a month has passed without a run.

score.py exits non-zero when a field misses the bar, so it can block a deploy.

Try it

The code, the 20 documents, our raw replies and the answer key are in the free download. You need Python and two packages; an API key only to run extractions. Scoring needs none.

Running the scripts overwrites the matching files in data/outputs/, so copy that folder first if you want to keep our runs.

python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install pydantic requests
python code/fetch_docs.py                            # optional: re-download the 20 documents from the Federal Register
python code/score.py data/outputs/*.jsonl            # re-score our runs, no API key needed (exits 1: our LLM runs fail the bar, and the publisher file skips three fields)
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...                            # OpenAI direct: gpt-5-nano until 11 Dec 2026, then gpt-6-luna
# or: export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=...                  # gateway: use openai/gpt-5-nano
python code/extract.py gpt-5-nano                    # OpenAI direct writes a new gpt-5-nano.jsonl beside ours
python code/extract.py gpt-5-nano --no-date-format   # the third run: no format: date
python code/regex_baseline.py                        # no LLM
python code/metadata_as_output.py                    # the publisher's own fields
python code/score.py data/outputs/*.jsonl            # seven outcomes per field; exits 1 on a FAIL or a skipped field
python code/plausible_dates.py data/outputs/openai__gpt-5-nano.jsonl   # drop out-of-window dates
python code/score.py data/outputs/plausible/openai__gpt-5-nano.jsonl   # the eight dates now score failed

To score any other tool (your own parser, a vendor's export, another model), write one JSON line per document with its document_number and a parsed object holding every field, null where empty, or parsed: null if the call failed. If your tool can't produce a field at all, list it under "not_scored" on every row; score.py then says so and exits non-zero unless you pass --allow-skip. Then run score.py on that file:

{"document_number": "2026-19757", "parsed": {"agency": "Federal Aviation Administration", "action": "Final rule; request for comments", "docket_id": "FAA-2026-11786", "rin": "2120-AA64", "effective_date": "2026-10-13", "comments_due": "2026-11-12"}}

For your own documents, edit FIELDS and DATE_FIELDS at the top of score.py, the model in schema.py and your answer_key.csv. In extract.py, also change the document list, SYSTEM and MAX_CHARS: it cuts each document at 8,000 characters, and a field past the cut usually scores missing, which looks like a model miss. The bar scales with your row count, rounded up, so under 20 rows it means every row.

Twenty checked rows outlast every model you will try on them.

Use those 20 rows to find problems. A tool or fix that passes them has earned a test on documents you haven't looked at, before it goes anywhere near production. Keep every document that fails, and score again whenever anything in the system changes. This week, key the first 20 and write your bar down before you score anything.

Prior work and further reading

  • The Durability Curve, Your AI Grader Is Only as Good as Its Answer Key: sets out a twenty-item check with a scoring sheet, counts false passes and false fails separately, and says to check the key before you blame the grader. This guide applies the same move to extraction.
  • Nancy Chinchor and Beth Sundheim, MUC-5 evaluation metrics (1993): the scoring categories, down to "spurious".
  • Strands Evals, structured-output evaluator: requires zero false alarms when there was nothing to find.
  • filing-extraction-benchmark: scores rules, an LLM and a hybrid that asks the model only where the rules abstain, all with one scorer.
  • Simon Willison, Structured data extraction, PyCon 2025 handout: schema extraction from a real FEMA briefing PDF.
  • DeepLearning.AI, Function-calling and data extraction with LLMs (Jiantao Jiao and Venkat Srinivasan of Nexusflow), with a "Structured Extraction" lesson on an open model.
  • Structured-output docs, all checked 13 November 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini.
  • The Durability Curve, Metric Validity Audit: a browser tool for "Your metric is green. Should you believe it?" Run your extraction score through it.

If someone on your team is about to ship an extraction because the JSON validated, send them this first.

title: iFixAi: an independent auditor for AI agents
description:
iFixAi

Most agent evaluations test speed, cost or prompt injection resistance. They do not answer the question that matters in production: is the agent doing the job it was hired for. iFixAi audits an agent by putting it in a simulation of your business, sending it real requests including ones that push past its role, and having a judge from a different provider grade the replies. A default run covers 10 inspections, with a full run covering 61, and the result is an A to F grade. An agent that can delete records, with a permission check the auditor cannot see, fails. Audit before you trust it with real work. It has 46,679 stars on GitHub, is Apache-2.0 licensed, and the latest release is v4.3.0.

What you get

  • A grade built on five pillars: fabrication, manipulation, deception, unpredictability and opacity, with three mandatory minimums (B01, B08 and P01) that cap the grade at D if any of them fails
  • A judge picked from a different provider than your agent, so the agent is never graded by its own model
  • Install with pip install ifixai (Python 3.10 or newer), and a demo run with no API key that shows the flow on a built-in demo agent
  • Reports in JSON and Markdown, so you can compare runs or gate CI with a minimum score, plus a plugin for Claude Code and Codex and a skill for Cursor, VS Code and more

The point is not a faster agent. It is an agent you can trust with real work. Run the default 10 first, read what failed and why, and only then decide what it is allowed to touch.

Repo: https://github.com/ifixai-ai/iFixAi

Quick poll

What would you use iFixAi for first?

  • Auditing my own agent before it ships
  • Running the 10-inspection default run first
  • Trying the demo agent with no API key
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found iFixAi interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: AI Agents Explained for Beginners: What an AI Agent Is, How It Works, and How It Differs From a Chatbot
description:
AI agents, explained for beginners.
Everyone uses the word.
Few people can say how an agent is different from a chatbot.

On the day I recorded the video, I had 47 Claude Code sessions open at the same time.
Each one had its own job.

I made a video about it.
This article has what the video has no room for: a table of chatbot vs workflow vs agent in Anthropic's own words, the five patterns Anthropic sees before you even need an agent, how the loop works inside Claude Code, the safety settings that decide what an agent may do without asking, and a step-by-step way to build your first one.

The short version

  • A chatbot answers. You ask, it replies, and you do the work.
  • An agent does the work. Anthropic defines agents as "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage".
  • A workflow sits in between. The tools are the same, but the steps are written in advance.
  • Inside, an agent is "typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop" (Anthropic).
  • Claude Code's docs name the loop's three phases: gather context, take action, verify results.
  • Anthropic's first advice is to find the simplest solution. Sometimes that means no agent at all.
  • Agents cost more, and their errors can compound. Anthropic recommends sandboxed testing and guardrails.
  • Hand over work with a clear finish line. Keep anything you cannot undo.

I have run my own company in Japan for 22 years.
Today, AI makes twelve videos and twelve carousel sets a day for my company.
So this is not theory for me.
I checked what I say in the video against Anthropic's article and the Claude Code docs.

What is an AI agent? Anthropic's definition

Anthropic's engineering article "Building effective agents" (December 19, 2024) draws one line.

Agents are "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks."

Workflows are "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths."

Anthropic calls both of them agentic systems.
Add the plain chatbot, and you get three kinds of thing that people all call "AI".

Chatbot Workflow Agent
Who decides the next step You Whoever wrote the path in advance The model
Uses tools No, it replies with text Yes, at fixed points Yes, it picks which ones and when
Sees the result of its own action No Only where a check was written in Yes, at each step
Who does the work You The system, along a fixed path The agent, until done or stopped
Good for Questions, explanations, ideas Well-defined tasks that should run the same way every time Open-ended tasks where you cannot predict the steps
Cost and risk Lowest Predictable Higher costs, potential for compounding errors

The last three rows come from Anthropic's own wording.
Workflows "offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks".
Agents are better "when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed at scale".

The Claude Code docs say the same thing from the other side.
"Without tools, Claude can only respond with text. With tools, Claude can act."

AI agent vs chatbot: the same request, two results

Ask a chatbot to fix a broken link on your website.

It tells you how.
Open the file.
Find the link.
Change it.
Then you do all of that yourself.

Ask an agent the same thing.

It opens the files, finds the link, fixes it, and checks the page again.

That is what Claude Code does.
The official overview: "Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with your development tools."

The "How Claude Code works" page adds that it is not only for code.
It "can help with anything you can do from the command line: writing docs, running builds, searching files, researching topics, and more."

AI agent vs workflow

A workflow follows a path someone wrote in advance.
An agent picks its own path.

This matters more than it sounds.
Anthropic's article spends most of its length on workflows, not agents.
Before you build an agent, it is worth knowing the five patterns Anthropic says it has "seen in production".

Pattern What it does When Anthropic says to use it Anthropic's example
Prompt chaining Each LLM call works on the output of the previous one, with checks in between The task splits cleanly into fixed subtasks Write marketing copy, then translate it
Routing Classifies the input and sends it to a specialized follow-up Distinct categories that are better handled separately Send general questions, refund requests and technical support to different processes
Parallelization Runs subtasks at the same time, or the same task several times Speed, or several attempts for higher confidence Several prompts review code for vulnerabilities
Orchestrator-workers A central LLM breaks down the task, hands parts to worker LLMs, and combines the results You cannot predict the subtasks in advance Changes across many files in a coding task
Evaluator-optimizer One LLM call writes, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loop Clear evaluation criteria, and refinement measurably helps Literary translation with a critic

All five start from one building block Anthropic calls the augmented LLM: a model with retrieval, tools and memory.

And Anthropic adds: "For many applications, however, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough."

How AI agents work: the loop

So what happens inside an agent?
Anthropic puts it simply.
Agents "are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop."

This is how I explain it in the video.
Look at the goal.
Pick a tool.
Run it.
Check the result.
Then decide the next step.
Repeat until it is done.

Claude Code's docs name the same loop with three phases: "gather context, take action, and verify results."
They give an example.
When you say "fix the failing tests," Claude might:

  1. Run the test suite to see what's failing
  2. Read the error output
  3. Search for the relevant source files
  4. Read those files to understand the code
  5. Edit the files to fix the issue
  6. Run the tests again to verify

Step 6 is the part a chatbot never does.
The agent checks its own work against the real world.
Anthropic calls this getting "ground truth" from the environment at each step.

The tools are what make the loop possible.
Claude Code's docs sort its built-in tools into five categories:

Category What Claude can do (Claude Code docs)
File operations Read files, edit code, create new files, rename and reorganize
Search Find files by pattern, search content with regex, explore codebases
Execution Run shell commands, start servers, run tests, use git
Web Search the web, fetch documentation, look up error messages
Code intelligence See type errors and warnings after edits, jump to definitions, find references (requires code intelligence plugins)

Anthropic also describes how an agent's task begins and ends.

  • It starts with a command from you, or a conversation with you.
  • Once the task is clear, the agent plans and works on its own.
  • It can come back to you for more information or a judgment call.
  • It can pause for your feedback at checkpoints, or when it gets stuck.
  • The task often ends when it is complete, but it is also common to add stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations.

You are part of the loop too.
In Claude Code, pressing Esc stops it immediately, and you can type a correction while it works.

My agents: one agent's day

Here is one of mine.
This one makes English videos.
The video above came from it.

It searches what people look up, reads the official sources, writes the script in English, and sends it to me for review.

After I say okay, it makes the voice, the screens and the video.
Then it checks its own work before I see it again.

Look at where the loop is.
It does not just write and stop.
It reads the sources before it writes, and it checks the finished video before it hands it back.

The other agents

The other sessions do other jobs.
Blog articles.
Social posts.
Newsletters.
Carousels.
Each one runs its own loop.

They do not talk to me all day.
They talk to each other.
One finishes a video and tells the next one to write the blog post about it.

Together, they make twelve videos and twelve carousel sets a day for my company.

The part most beginner guides skip

Anthropic itself says: "we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed. This might mean not building agentic systems at all."

Its summary is even plainer.
"Start with simple prompts, optimize them with comprehensive evaluation, and add multi-step agentic systems only when simpler solutions fall short."

So before you build an agent, ask in this order:

Question If yes
Does one good prompt, with the right examples, already get the result? Use a chatbot. No agent.
Are the steps the same every time? Use a workflow, or a plain script.
Do the steps depend on what it finds along the way? Now an agent makes sense.

Why not always use an agent?
Anthropic: "The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors."

One wrong step, then the next step builds on it.
A chatbot that is wrong gives you one wrong answer.
An agent that is wrong can take ten more actions on top of it.

How I keep control

Anthropic's advice: "We recommend extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with the appropriate guardrails."

Here is what that means in Claude Code, in the docs' own terms.

What can be undone, and what cannot

Claude Code snapshots a file before it edits it.
Press Esc twice to rewind, or ask it to undo.

But the docs draw a hard line: "Actions that affect remote systems (databases, APIs, deployments) can't be checkpointed. You control those with your permission mode and permission rules."

That one sentence is the reason for most of my rules.

Permission modes

Press Shift+Tab to cycle through them.

Mode What it does (Claude Code docs)
Manual Claude asks before file edits and shell commands
Accept edits Claude edits files and runs common filesystem commands like mkdir and mv without asking, still asks for other commands
Plan Claude explores and proposes a plan without editing your source files
Auto A classifier reviews most actions in the background and blocks the risky ones instead of asking you

Permission rules

You can write allow, ask and deny rules in .claude/settings.json.
The docs: "Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow."
So a deny rule always wins.

This example is from the docs.
It lets Claude run npm scripts and git commits without asking, and refuses commands that begin with git push.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(git commit *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Bash(git push *)"
    ]
  }
}

Hooks

Hooks are shell commands Claude Code runs at fixed points.
The docs say they give "deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them."
A hook on PreToolUse runs before a tool call, and can block it by exiting with code 2.

I have 70 hook scripts.

Not all of them stop commands.
In my settings they are registered 77 times, and 48 of those registrations run before a tool call, where they can stop a risky command before it runs.
The rest check work after the fact, or when a session ends.

My okay at the end

And nothing goes out to the public without my okay.
The agents do the work.
I keep the final say.

AI agent use cases: what to hand over

Hand an agent work with a clear finish line, where it can check itself.
Research.
First drafts.
Checking a list against the rules.

Anthropic says agents add the most value for tasks that "require both conversation and action, have clear success criteria, enable feedback loops, and integrate meaningful human oversight."

It names two areas where its customers found agents most promising.

Use case Why it fits, in Anthropic's words
Customer support Support "naturally" follows a conversation while needing outside information and actions. Tools can pull customer data, order history and knowledge base articles. Refunds and ticket updates can be handled programmatically. Success can be measured through user-defined resolutions.
Coding agents Code can be verified through automated tests. Agents can iterate using test results as feedback. The problem is well-defined. Output quality can be measured objectively.

Even there, Anthropic adds: "human review remains crucial".

Here is how I split the work in my own company.

Job What the agent does What I keep
Video Searches what people look up, reads official sources, writes the script, makes the voice, screens and video, checks its own work The okay on the script and the okay before it goes public
Blog articles Turns a finished video into an article and checks it against the rules The okay before it goes public
Social posts, carousels, newsletters Drafts and checks them The okay before they go out
Anything with money, deletion or a real customer Asks me first The decision itself

What never to hand over

Anything you cannot undo.
Sending money.
Deleting data.
Emailing a real customer.

These are exactly the "remote systems" the Claude Code docs say cannot be checkpointed.
A file edit can be rewound.
A sent email cannot.

My agents have to ask me first for every one of those.
Every time.

Build your first AI agent, step by step

Pick the task

Pick one task you do every week, the same way, that bores you.
Then run it through the three questions above.
If one prompt or a fixed workflow already does it, you are done, and that is a good result.

Write down what done looks like

An agent stops when it knows it is done.
So write it down: what the finished output is, where it goes, and how it can check itself.
"Clear success criteria", in Anthropic's words.

Give it only the tools it needs, and keep your okay

If you use Claude Code, this is how those steps map to its own features.

  • Install it. The overview page gives curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash for macOS, Linux and WSL, with separate commands for Windows. Most surfaces require a Claude subscription or an Anthropic Console account.
  • Start it in the folder for the task: cd your-project, then claude.
  • Run /init to generate a starter CLAUDE.md, then write your "done" into it. The docs: put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md rather than relying on conversation history.
  • Start in Manual mode, so it asks before file edits and shell commands. Switch with Shift+Tab.
  • Open /permissions and allow only the commands this task needs. Deny the ones it must never run.
  • If something must be blocked every time, without depending on the model to remember, use a PreToolUse hook.
  • Watch the first runs. Press Esc to stop it, or type a correction while it works.
  • Keep the final okay before anything leaves your machine.

Then add the second one

Do not start with 47.
Start with one.
Add the next one when the first one is reliable.

Checklist before you hand a task to an agent

  • Could one good prompt do this? Then you do not need an agent.
  • Are the steps the same every time? Then a workflow or a script is simpler.
  • Is there a clear finish line the agent can check by itself?
  • Is "done" written down where the agent reads it every session?
  • Does it have only the tools this task needs?
  • Is anything in the task impossible to undo: money, deletion, a message to a real person, a deploy? Make those ask you first, or deny them.
  • Is there a hard stop for the things that must never happen, not just an instruction?
  • Did you watch it run before you stopped watching?
  • Do you still give the final okay before anything goes public?

Anthropic's three principles

Anthropic ends its article with three principles it follows when it builds agents:

  • Maintain simplicity in your agent's design.
  • Prioritize transparency by explicitly showing the agent's planning steps.
  • Carefully craft your agent-computer interface (ACI) through thorough tool documentation and testing.

One note on dates.
Anthropic's article is from December 2024, and the page itself now says much of the tooling it describes has changed.
The definitions and the advice above are the parts I checked against the current Claude Code docs.

An agent is not a smarter chatbot.
It is a loop you trust with one job.

Sources (official pages, read November 6, 2026):

  • Anthropic, "Building effective agents", December 19, 2024 (anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)
  • Claude Code Docs, "Overview" (code.claude.com/docs/en/overview)
  • Claude Code Docs, "How Claude Code works" (code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works)
  • Claude Code Docs, "Configure permissions" (code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)
  • Claude Code Docs, "Automate actions with hooks" (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide)

title: Anthropic & OpenAI both filed for IPO: what it means for everyday AI users
description:
Two of the world's biggest AI labs made their move to the public markets in the same week. Before you write it off as a Wall Street story, here's what actually changes for the people who use these tools every day.

My first reaction was: of course they did.

My second was: wait, both of them? In the same week?

Anthropic, maker of Claude, and OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, have both filed IPO paperwork. Between them they've raised more than $50 billion in private capital. And both started from the same unusual premise: we may be building something dangerous, so we'd rather be the ones building it carefully.

Now they're heading to the public markets, and I keep turning that over, because going public is never a neutral event. It changes who a company actually answers to.

Most coverage fixates on valuations and investor returns. That isn't what I want to write about. I want to look at what changes for the person who uses Claude to draft emails, leans on ChatGPT to prepare for meetings, or relies on these tools to get through a workday.

Because something does change. Not right away, but reliably. If you use these products regularly, you should know what to expect.

The IPO machine changes what a company cares about

Private companies enjoy a freedom that public ones lose. They can absorb a bad quarter without a stock-price cliff, bet on products that won't pay off for three years, and tell a board of twenty people "trust us," often successfully.

Public companies answer to markets, and markets are impatient.

Once an S-1 is filed, the company enters a world of quarterly earnings calls, institutional shareholders, analyst coverage, and revenue guidance. Every three months, leadership faces the market and explains whether the business is growing fast enough. If it isn't, the stock falls. When the stock falls, options lose value, and people leave. When key people leave, the product suffers.

That pressure doesn't stay in the boardroom. It passes down through layers of management until it lands somewhere users can feel it, usually in the product.

Going public doesn't mean a company stops caring about what it builds. It means the company must care about what it builds and hit revenue targets every 90 days, in public, at the same time.
I've watched versions of this happen to companies I used and liked, and the pattern is consistent. Free tiers get narrower and upsells get pushier. Features that don't drive conversion lose priority, and the user experience slowly bends toward the spreadsheet.

Anthropic and OpenAI won't be immune. No company is.

The safety mission gets expensive, fast

This is the part I keep returning to, and I'll be blunt: it's the part that actually worries me.

Both companies built serious safety research practices. Anthropic published its Constitutional AI framework, and OpenAI funded alignment research for years. These aren't PR exercises. They're slow, costly, technically difficult efforts that deliver results on a timeline unrelated to quarterly earnings.

Safety research doesn't ship features or lower the cost per query, and it rarely appears on a slide with a growth chart.

A public company can fund safety research. What it can't do is ask analysts to be patient because the safer model isn't finished yet.
Anthropic's founding story is worth recalling here. Several of its founders left OpenAI in 2021 precisely because they believed safety was being traded for speed, and they started Anthropic to do things differently. That intention hasn't vanished. But an IPO sets it against a new set of obligations, and obligations backed by quarterly reporting tend to win out over time.

Dario Amodei has written openly about the tension between commercial pressure and responsible AI development. Once Anthropic is public, that tension stops being philosophical and becomes financial.

I don't think either company will gut its safety team. That would be reckless and reputationally catastrophic. But resources will compete harder, and safety work that doesn't translate into shipped features will lose some of those contests.

How this plays out at the product level

Let's get concrete, because abstract talk about "market incentives" means little until you can picture what actually changes.

Free tiers will tighten. Claude and ChatGPT both offer genuinely useful free access today, and that's user-acquisition spending. Once Anthropic and OpenAI are public and need to show revenue per user, free access turns into a cost to minimize rather than a feature to promote. Expect lower message limits, older models on free plans, and more friction before you reach the paywall.

Paid plans will probably get pricier. At the very least, what you get for the current price will quietly shrink. Packaging will change before the number does, and you'll notice when a feature you relied on moves up a tier.

Enterprise customers will matter more than individual users. A hundred-seat enterprise contract is worth more, and easier to forecast, than ten thousand individual subscriptions. Public companies need predictable revenue, and enterprise delivers it, while consumer subscriptions are lumpy and churn easily. That doesn't mean individual users get ignored. It means the product roadmap tilts.

Data and privacy terms will come under closer scrutiny. Being public brings SEC filings, shareholder lawsuits, and regulatory attention. That's not entirely bad, since it creates a paper trail and legal accountability that didn't exist while these companies were private. Watch for terms-of-service updates in the six to twelve months after listing.

What competition between two public AI companies looks like

Not all of this is bad news, and some of it may genuinely help users.

Two public AI companies competing for users in front of the same investors is a different dynamic from two private ones doing the same. Wall Street will compare them head to head, with analysts tracking user growth, churn, and average revenue per user. The moment one company loses ground on any of those measures, pressure builds to respond.

That's a reason to keep pricing competitive. If Anthropic raises prices sharply and users migrate to ChatGPT, its user numbers look bad next quarter. If OpenAI degrades its free tier and Claude holds steady, OpenAI's growth story weakens. That competitive pressure sets a floor on how bad things can get for users, as long as neither company reaches total dominance.

The scenario to watch for is consolidation. If one company pulls far ahead in users or revenue, pressure on the other becomes severe, and desperate companies make decisions that hurt users. So the healthiest outcome for people who use these tools daily is a close race between two well-funded, well-run competitors.

That's what we have right now. Whether an IPO helps or hurts that balance is genuinely unclear.

Five things worth doing before pricing changes arrive

You have a window right now. The products are still in growth mode, free tiers are still generous, and pricing hasn't yet adjusted to public-market pressure. A few moves are worth making.

Export anything you care about. That means chat histories, custom instructions, saved outputs, and any configuration you've built inside these platforms. Companies in transition reset things and data policies change, so keep local copies of anything you'd hate to lose.
Get to know the alternatives now, not in a crisis. Google Gemini, Mistral, and models built on Meta's Llama are mature enough for serious use. If pricing or terms change in ways you dislike, switching is far easier when you've already practiced.
Read the terms-of-service updates when they arrive. They will, probably within a year of listing. Companies bury the meaningful changes in paragraph four of a document nobody opens, so set a reminder to actually read it.
If you're already paying and happy, consider locking in an annual plan. Software prices tend to move in one direction after an IPO. If the product genuinely works for you, an annual commitment at today's rates is worth considering.
Follow the earnings calls once the companies are public. I know, it sounds tedious. But earnings calls are where companies say what they actually care about, in plain language and under legal obligation. A single call will tell you more about the product roadmap than a year of blog posts.

The line I keep coming back to

At some point in their history, both companies said something most companies never say: we might be building something that could go wrong in serious ways, and we want to be the ones doing it carefully.

It's an odd thing to put in a pitch. Most companies just build the product and call it safe.

An IPO doesn't erase that intention. It does put it in a room with shareholders, quarterly reports, and analyst calls, and asks it to compete. Over a five-year horizon, I genuinely don't know who wins that fight. I've seen mission-driven companies hold their values under public pressure, and I've seen others hollow out so slowly that nobody noticed until the product was unrecognizable.

What I do know is that the people best positioned to hold these companies accountable are their users, not their investors. Users who understand what changed, watch how the product moves, and speak up when it moves in the wrong direction.

That starts with knowing what changed. Now you do.

Enjoyed this read? Be sure to follow me for more stories that make people feel things. You can also connect with me on LinkedIn or Telegram @kawsarlog for more updates on my work.

I do freelance scraping projects, so if you need some data collected feel free to contact me on LinkedIn or email at hi@kawsarlog.com

title: Five ways a beginner's agent loop breaks
description:
Most beginner agents I've come across look something like this:

while True:
    reply = llm(messages, tools)
    if reply.tool_call:
        result = run_tool(reply.tool_call)
        messages.append(result)
    else:
        return reply.text

It runs fine in a demo, then fails in five very predictable ways.

1. No clear stop condition

The model keeps making tool calls because nothing explicitly tells it when to stop. Fix: set a step limit and add a dedicated "finish" tool, so stopping becomes an intentional decision by the model.

2. Repeating the same failed call

A tool returns an error, and the model tries again with exactly the same arguments. Fix: feed the error back unchanged and track repeated calls. After three identical attempts, stop and replan, or ask the user.

3. Errors that disappear

run_tool catches an exception and returns "". The model continues as if nothing happened and often makes up a result. Fix: treat errors as data. Return them as readable text so the model can understand and respond to them.

4. Context that keeps expanding

Every tool result gets added in full, and by step 20 the original instructions are lost in the noise. Fix: shorten or summarize earlier results, while keeping the actual task visible at the top.

5. Claiming "done" without checking

The model announces that the task is finished, but nobody verifies it. Fix: add a verification step before accepting the answer: run a test, execute a query, or have another prompt review the result.

I've been working on Way of the Agent, a game-based course about agent engineering, and these five problems appear as daily exercises: a quick scenario - "your agent keeps repeating the same tool call", "a tool call fails, how should your loop respond?" - followed by four possible solutions to pick from. Choosing the correct solution turned out to test understanding better than answering questions about definitions.

You can start for free, with a subscription unlocking the complete path, available on web, Android and iOS, in 8 languages: https://wayofagent.app

What failure would you put at number six? I'm gathering real-world examples.

title: Fleet Tracking and Remote Diagnostics: IoT Product Development for Connected Vehicles
description:
Managing a fleet is about more than knowing where vehicles are. Fleet operators also need to understand how vehicles are being driven, whether components are performing as expected, and when maintenance may be required. Traditional tracking systems provide location updates, but connected vehicle technology can offer a much broader operational picture.

By combining GPS, onboard diagnostics, sensors, and cloud-based platforms, the Internet of Things (IoT) makes it possible to monitor vehicles remotely and use operational data to improve fleet decisions. The real opportunity, however, is not collecting the largest amount of data. It is collecting information that helps operators act at the right time.

1. Fleet Tracking Goes Beyond GPS Location

GPS tracking remains the foundation of most fleet monitoring systems. A connected tracking unit can transmit vehicle coordinates, speed, direction, and trip information to a centralized platform.

When combined with additional data, fleet managers can:

  • Monitor vehicle locations and route progress.
  • Identify unauthorized or unexpected vehicle use.
  • Review idle time and driving patterns.
  • Compare planned routes with actual journeys.
  • Improve dispatch coordination and delivery visibility.

For larger fleets, location information can be combined with geofencing. A notification can be generated when a vehicle enters or leaves a defined area, helping teams monitor depot arrivals, delivery zones, and restricted locations.

However, GPS data should not be treated as perfectly continuous. Tunnels, dense urban areas, poor network coverage, and device faults can affect location accuracy or transmission frequency.

2. Remote Diagnostics Helps Identify Vehicle Problems Earlier

Remote diagnostics adds another layer of visibility by collecting information from a vehicle's electronic systems. Depending on vehicle compatibility and the installed hardware, data may come from the onboard diagnostics interface, CAN bus, or additional sensors.

Useful parameters can include:

  • Engine temperature and operating conditions.
  • Battery voltage and charging performance.
  • Diagnostic trouble codes.
  • Fuel consumption and engine performance indicators.
  • Selected component temperatures or pressure readings.

When a vehicle reports a diagnostic fault, the platform can notify maintenance teams and help them prioritize inspections. Historical readings can also reveal recurring issues that might otherwise go unnoticed.

It is important to distinguish between fault detection and fault prediction. A diagnostic code can indicate an existing or detected problem, but predicting a future failure requires suitable historical data, validated models, and vehicle-specific context.

3. How Connected Vehicle IoT Architecture Works

A typical connected fleet system has four main layers:

  • Vehicle hardware: GPS modules, telematics control units, onboard diagnostic interfaces, and sensors collect vehicle information.
  • Connectivity: Cellular networks such as 4G or 5G transmit information to remote platforms. Bluetooth or other local connections may support nearby device communication.
  • Cloud or edge processing: Incoming data is organized, stored, and analyzed. Edge processing can handle selected alerts locally when low latency or intermittent connectivity is a concern.
  • Fleet dashboard: Web and mobile applications display vehicle locations, diagnostic alerts, trip histories, and maintenance information.

An experienced IoT development company can help connect these layers while accounting for hardware compatibility, communication protocols, security, and scalability.

4. Why IoT Product Development Requires Careful Planning

A fleet tracking product may appear straightforward, but its reliability depends on decisions made early in development. Vehicle models differ, diagnostic interfaces are not identical, and telematics devices operate under demanding power and environmental conditions.

A practical IoT product development process should consider:

  • Compatibility with vehicle models and diagnostic interfaces.
  • Accurate GPS positioning and dependable data transmission.
  • Secure device identity and encrypted communication.
  • Local data buffering during network outages.
  • Remote firmware updates and device health monitoring.
  • Dashboard usability and integration with fleet or maintenance software.

Businesses evaluating IoT development services should also ask how the solution handles missing readings, duplicate messages, faulty sensors, and disconnected devices. These situations are common in real-world deployments and should not be treated as unusual exceptions.

5. Practical Benefits and Limitations

Connected vehicle systems can help fleet operators improve route visibility, investigate fuel and idle-time patterns, organize maintenance, and reduce manual reporting. They may also help businesses identify vehicles that require attention before a minor issue becomes a costly disruption.

But technology alone cannot guarantee lower operating costs. Poorly calibrated sensors, inconsistent vehicle data, unreliable connectivity, and excessive alerts can reduce the usefulness of a system.

Data privacy is another consideration. Location and driver-related information should be collected for defined purposes, protected through appropriate access controls, and retained according to applicable requirements.

A limited pilot across a representative group of vehicles is often the best starting point. It allows operators to test data accuracy, device durability, alert quality, and actual maintenance workflows before expanding deployment.

6. Evaluating an IoT Development Partner in Noida, India

Companies researching connected vehicle solutions in Noida, India, may encounter providers with different levels of hardware, software, and automotive integration experience. A useful evaluation should examine their ability to work with embedded firmware, GPS and telematics hardware, CAN bus data, cloud platforms, dashboards, and remote device management.

HashStudioz is one provider whose published IoT portfolio includes automotive applications such as fleet monitoring, remote diagnostics, connected vehicles, and GPS tracking. Its IoT development page also describes capabilities across embedded systems, gateways, cloud connectivity, dashboards, and hardware engineering.

For context, the HashStudioz homepage displayed 100+ happy clients, 300+ dedicated developers, 10.0K+ smart devices, and 15+ countries served when checked on November 19, 2026. Its IoT page separately displayed 50+ global clients, 200+ projects delivered, and 350+ IoT and software engineers. These are company-reported figures, not independently verified performance measures.

Such numbers offer background, but they should not replace a review of relevant automotive case studies, technical architecture, security practices, and post-deployment support.

Conclusion

Fleet tracking and remote diagnostics can give businesses a clearer view of vehicle operations, but their success depends on reliable hardware, useful data, and well-designed software. GPS tracking establishes location visibility; diagnostics adds insight into vehicle condition; and connected dashboards bring the information together for operational decisions.

In my view, the strongest solutions are those built around specific fleet problems rather than an excessive list of features. A carefully tested pilot, followed by measurable improvements in visibility and maintenance planning, is a more convincing path to connected fleet management.

title: AI Customer Support Benchmark: Resolution Performance and Cost Analysis.
description:
I wouldn't trust an AI customer support dashboard that claims 90% automation without asking one question: 90% of what?

Conversations handled? Tickets closed? Or customer problems actually solved?

Those numbers can tell very different stories.

An AI chatbot might answer 900 out of 1,000 customer requests, yet still leave hundreds of people without a working solution. The dashboard looks impressive, but the support team continues dealing with repeat tickets, failed refunds, and unresolved account issues.

That's what caught my attention while reading YourGPT's AI customer support benchmark. It looks beyond automation percentages and considers verified resolutions, human involvement, and the total cost of support.

I wanted to examine the numbers from a developer's perspective. What should count as a successful AI resolution? How do we measure it? And when does automating support actually save money?

Problem With a 90% Automation Rate

Let's say a company receives 1,000 support requests.

Its AI chatbot handles 900 conversations without immediately transferring them to a human.

The company reports a 90% automation rate.

But what happened to those 900 customers?

Some probably received the information they needed. Others may have abandoned the conversation, received an incorrect answer, or returned later with the same problem.

An automation rate alone doesn't tell us.

These metrics often get mixed together:

Metric What it tells us
Automation rate How much work or interaction is handled automatically
Containment rate How many conversations avoid human takeover
Resolution rate How many customer issues are successfully completed
AI-only resolution How many issues AI resolves without human involvement
Escalation rate How often ownership transfers to human support

Here's a simple example.

A customer asks an AI assistant to cancel a subscription.

The chatbot explains how to cancel it and ends the conversation.

Technically, the AI handled the request. But if the customer expected the chatbot to cancel the subscription, the job isn't finished.

Now imagine the chatbot says, "Your subscription has been cancelled," but the billing API actually failed.
