A public raise can strengthen a company’s ability to fund that system, but it does not automatically guarantee lower API prices, better uptime, or a particular model roadmap.

Going public did not make Anthropic a conventional one-share, one-vote company

The filing also lays out a distinctive governance system. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, whose stated purpose is to balance stockholder interests with the interests of people affected by its conduct and the responsible development of advanced AI. Its Class A shares carry one vote each, but that is not the whole picture. A single Class F share held by an entity organized by the founders has voting power equal to 50.1% on general stockholder matters, while the Long-Term Benefit Trust’s Class T share gives it authority to elect and remove directors who together make up a majority of the board.

So the IPO creates a public market and new disclosure obligations, while leaving substantial control mechanisms outside ordinary public-share voting. That may be part of how Anthropic intends to preserve its mission; it also means “publicly traded” does not simply translate into public investors controlling the company.

What to watch next

The useful test is not the amount raised alone. It is whether the company can turn committed infrastructure into services customers keep paying for, while growing revenue efficiently enough to support ongoing compute and research costs. Reuters reported that Anthropic shares closed at $88.91 on November 20, after a volatile debut and down 8.5% from the previous day’s close. Catalyst Funds chief investment officer David Miller told Reuters: “Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth.” That short-term movement is no verdict on the company, but it is a reminder that record-size financing does not settle the market’s questions about AI spending and returns.

Anthropic’s IPO and concurrent placement put two facts in the same frame: frontier AI attracts extraordinary pools of capital, and the infrastructure appetite disclosed alongside that capital is larger still. For developers, the signal is about the shape of the industry, not a promise about any single product. The next meaningful evidence will come from the company’s operating results, investment choices, and the value customers get from the systems those investments support.

title: Hidden Prompt Injections in Financial PDFs, and Where a Scrub Step Fits
description:
A QA engineer pointed an internal LLM tool at financial PDFs (SEC filings, account statements) and made it report numbers that weren't in the document. The tool did what it was built to do. It read the PDF, and the attacker had written some of the PDF for it.

This is a research write-up, not a breach. The author, writing at tomclancy.info, demonstrated the attack against a tool that parses financial documents, then built a set of mechanical PDF-level detectors to catch it. The piece got almost no traction on HN (1 point, 0 comments), which is a shame, because the underlying problem is one most document-ingestion pipelines have.

How the attack worked

The demonstrated techniques all do the same thing: put text in the PDF that an LLM will see and a human reviewer won't.

  • White-on-white text. Instructions rendered in the page background color.
  • Zero-height text. Text with no vertical extent, so nothing visible is drawn.
  • Off-page text. Content positioned outside the visible page area.
  • Fake footnotes. Visible-looking footnotes instructing the model to report fabricated numbers.

The goal in the demo was to get the model to state numbers the document doesn't contain. For a tool people use to read filings and statements, wrong numbers delivered confidently are the worst outcome. A reviewer skimming the rendered PDF sees a normal document. The text extractor feeding the LLM sees the normal document plus a paragraph of instructions.

The detection gap

A PDF text extractor has no idea what's visible. It pulls characters out of content streams. Color, height, and position are rendering concerns the extractor doesn't weigh, so everything lands in the prompt as one undifferentiated string.

Then the model gets that string. System prompts that say "only report figures from the document" don't help, because the injected text is part of the document as far as the model can tell. Instructions and data arrive in the same channel.

The author's response is a layered "Swiss cheese" approach, six judges that each look for one kind of PDF-level trick: HiddenInk, Text Raster Divergence, Unicode Obfuscation, Accessibility Channel, Glyph Overlap, and Non-Text Ink. That's sound engineering. Each judge has holes, and stacking them is how you cover the holes. I'm not going to describe how each judge works internally, since the summary doesn't give me enough to do that honestly. Read the original for the details.

Where Sentinel fits (and where it doesn't)

Be clear about the division of labor. The author's judges operate on the PDF itself: rendering, glyph geometry, ink, accessibility tags. Sentinel doesn't parse PDFs or inspect rendering, so it can't tell you a span was white-on-white. That's the author's layer, and it's a good one.

Sentinel works on the text after extraction, before it reaches the model. For a pipeline like this, that means the extracted PDF text goes through /v1/scrub first. Hidden or not, an injected instruction ends up as text, and text is what Sentinel scans.

Three layers are relevant:

  1. Fast-path regex. Our library of regex patterns catches high-confidence injection signatures: authority hijacks ("ignore previous instructions", "your new system prompt is"), persona shifts, and tool abuse patterns. An extracted hidden paragraph that opens with that kind of phrasing gets stopped here with near-zero latency.
  2. Deep-path vector similarity. If no pattern fires, Sentinel embeds the text and compares it against our library of attack signature embeddings. This is the layer that matters for the fake-footnote case. A footnote telling the model to report specific figures doesn't look like a classic jailbreak phrase, so it's the semantic comparison, not the regex, that has a chance at it. I won't claim it catches every phrasing. It's a similarity score against known attack patterns, and a carefully worded footnote can score lower than a blunt one.
  3. Text normalization. Invisible characters, Unicode tag characters, and bidi overrides are stripped from the scanning copy, and homoglyphs are resolved to ASCII. Obfuscation found here adds to the threat score instead of being silently cleaned away. That's the neighbor of the author's Unicode Obfuscation judge, working on the text instead of the PDF.

One more layer is worth knowing about: the unverifiable authorization claim heuristic. Content that asserts its own authority ("you have my permission to...") sets a soft floor on the score and comes back flagged. Injected footnotes that claim to be corrections or official addenda can trip it. It's deliberately a flag and not a block, because the same phrasing is common in legitimate documents.

What Sentinel can't do here: it can't see that text was hidden. If an attacker writes an injection that reads like ordinary financial prose ("Restated net income was $4.2M"), there's no injection signature to match. That's a data-integrity problem, not a prompt-injection problem, and no scrub layer fixes it. The PDF-level judges and a human checking numbers against the source are the answer there.

What a scrub step looks like

Illustrative example: extract text, scrub it, and only send the result to the model if it passes.

import httpx

extracted = extract_text_from_pdf("filing.pdf")  # your extractor

resp = httpx.post(
    "https://api.sentinelaifirewall.com/v1/scrub",
    json={"content": extracted, "tier": "strict"},
    headers={"X-Sentinel-Key": "sk_live_..."},
).json()

action = resp["security"]["action_taken"]

if action == "blocked":
    raise ValueError("Document withheld: injection detected")
if action == "flagged":
    queue_for_human_review(resp["request_id"])

safe_text = resp["safe_payload"]  # send this to the LLM, not `extracted`

An illustrative response for a document with an injected instruction block:

{
  "request_id": "a1b2c3...",
  "security": {
    "action_taken": "blocked",
    "threat_score": 0.91
  },
  "safe_payload": "[SENTINEL BLOCKED]: Article withheld — fast-path prompt injection detected. Matched: \"...\"."
}

Note that safe_payload on a block is a descriptive placeholder, not null. Branch on action_taken, and log the placeholder if you like.

If you're feeding many filings through, /v1/scrub/batch (Teams and Enterprise) takes up to 100 items per request, so you can scan at ingestion time instead of per query.

Takeaway

Treat extracted document text as untrusted input, the same way you'd treat a web form field. If your pipeline goes PDF to extractor to LLM with nothing in between, add a scrub step between the extractor and the model today. Pair it with checks at the PDF layer like the ones in the original write-up, because they cover things a text-level scan can't see, and Sentinel covers things they can't. Neither catches plausible-looking wrong numbers, so keep a human verifying figures that matter.

Sentinel has a free Starter tier (100 requests/month, no credit card): sentinelaifirewall.com

Sources

  • Hiding prompt injections in PDFs, and six judges that catch them

AI-assisted draft or imaging, human-curated, reviewed and edited.

title: Agentes LLM: observabilidad para email de prueba
description:
Un agente LLM que completa un registro, solicita una verificación y espera un email parece sencillo hasta que falla. El modelo dice que terminó, el navegador muestra un timeout y el runner solo conserva una captura de pantalla. El equipo sabe que algo pasó, pero no sabe si falló el agente, la API, la entrega o la aserción.

La solución no es pedirle al modelo que “sea mas cuidadoso”. Es diseñar una frontera observable entre el agente y el sistema de email. En este artículo propongo un contrato pequeño: un identificador de correlación, estados explícitos y evidencia suficiente para reconstruir cada ejecución.

El problema: el agente ve el síntoma

En un flujo típico hay al menos cuatro relojes:

  1. El agente decide qué acción ejecutar.
  2. La aplicación acepta la solicitud y crea un evento.
  3. El proveedor de email entrega el mensaje al fixture.
  4. El test consulta el buzón y valida el enlace.

Si solo registramos “email no recibido”, mezclamos cuatro causas distintas. El diagnóstico se vuelve una conversación de opiniones. Ademas, un reintento puede crear un segundo mensaje y esconder el fallo original.

Un buen primer checkpoint es definir un correlation_id antes de que el agente haga la primera acción. Ese valor viaja por la interfaz web, la API, el evento de email y la consulta al buzón. El agente no necesita conocer todos los detalles internos; necesita recibir estados que pueda interpretar.

Un contrato de observabilidad

El contrato puede expresarse como una pequeña máquina de estados:

CREATED -> ACTION_SENT -> EMAIL_ACCEPTED -> EMAIL_VISIBLE -> LINK_ASSERTED
                    \-> FAILED

Cada transición debería tener cuatro campos:

  • correlation_id: identifica la ejecución completa.
  • state: el estado nuevo, no una descripción libre.
  • observed_at: hora del componente que produjo el evento.
  • evidence: datos mínimos, como un message_id, código HTTP o motivo de espera.

Esto complementa un contrato de espera para emails de prueba: la espera deja de ser un bucle opaco y pasa a ser una operación con resultado explicable. Si el fixture tiene caducidad, conviene modelarla también; los fixtures de email que expiran en FastAPI muestran por que el ciclo de vida debe estar en el contrato y no solo en un helper del test.

Flujo de ejecución con una sola correlación

Imaginemos un agente que prueba el onboarding de una aplicación. Antes de abrir el navegador, el runner crea una ejecución:

{
  "correlation_id": "run-8f31",
  "scenario": "onboarding",
  "email_fixture": "qa-8f31@example.test",
  "deadline_seconds": 45
}

El agente ejecuta la acción de signup y recibe ACTION_SENT. La aplicación registra el mismo correlation_id cuando acepta el evento. Luego el adaptador de email asocia el message_id con esa correlación. Finalmente, el lector del fixture devuelve EMAIL_VISIBLE o FAILED con una razón concreta.

La arquitectura importa: el LLM debe consumir un resumen de estado, mientras que el sistema conserva el evento completo. Por ejemplo, el modelo puede recibir “email visible después de 4,2 s; enlace encontrado”, pero el almacén de trazas conserva timestamps, intentos, proveedor y hash del contenido. Así se reduce el ruido del prompt sin perder evidencia para depurar.

Implementación mínima

Un adaptador de polling no necesita ser sofisticado. Lo importante es que clasifique el resultado y no esconda todos los problemas detrás de sleep(5):

def wait_for_email(client, correlation_id, deadline):
    while clock.now() < deadline:
        message = client.find(correlation_id=correlation_id)
        if message is not None:
            return {"state": "EMAIL_VISIBLE", "message_id": message.id}
        clock.wait(1)
    return {"state": "FAILED", "reason": "delivery_deadline_exceeded"}

En producción de pruebas, también registraría el número de consultas y el último estado conocido. Una frase como “no llegó” ayuda poco; “la API aceptó el evento, pero no hubo message_id en 45 segundos” ya apunta al componente correcto.

Hay que reservar algunos nombres de estado y documentarlos. Si cada integración inventa MAIL_OK, DELIVERED y FOUND para significar lo mismo, los paneles terminan siendo dificil de comparar. Es mejor una lista pequeña y estable, aunque al principio parezca menos flexible.

Qué medir y qué no

Las métricas más útiles son latencia de aceptación, latencia hasta visibilidad, porcentaje de estados terminales y distribución de causas de fallo. También conviene medir cuántos reintentos hizo el agente; un flujo que “pasa” después de cuatro intentos puede estar consumiendo un presupuesto de fiabilidad.

No hace falta enviar el cuerpo completo del email al prompt. Puede contener datos sensibles y además aumenta el coste de contexto. Un asunto normalizado, el identificador del mensaje y una lista de enlaces extraídos suelen bastar para la decisión. Para depuración, guarda el artefacto con retención corta y acceso restringido.

Las búsquedas humanas generan variantes como temp gamil com y tepm mail com. Deben tratarse como texto de consulta, nunca como una razón para relajar la validación del dominio o aceptar cualquier mensaje parecido.

Checklist de implementación

  • Crear el correlation_id antes de la primera acción del agente.
  • Propagarlo por UI, API, evento y fixture.
  • Definir estados terminales y razones de fallo.
  • Separar el resumen que lee el LLM de la traza completa.
  • Registrar message_id, latencias, intentos y deadline.
  • Hacer que los reintentos sean idempotentes.
  • Expirar los fixtures y borrar artefactos según una política clara.

El resultado es una frontera de email que se puede observar, probar y explicar. No elimina los fallos de entrega, pero evita que cada fallo se convierta en una adivinanza del agente.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Debo dar toda la traza al LLM?

No. Dale el estado actual, la razón de fallo y la siguiente acción permitida. Conserva la traza completa fuera del prompt para auditoría y análisis.

¿Un timeout siempre significa que el proveedor falló?

No. Puede haber fallado la publicación del evento, el filtro del fixture, la correlación o el reloj del test. Los estados intermedios permiten distinguirlos.

¿Cuándo es suficiente este diseño?

Cuando una ejecución fallida puede asignarse a un componente sin abrir cinco sistemas distintos. Si todavía no se puede, falta una transición o evidencia en el contrato.

title: No proof, no bug: making an AI code reviewer prove each defect with a failing test
description:
When a coding agent finishes a change, the usual "review" is the same model reading its own output. It tends to agree with itself.

During Meta's AI developer hackathon I tried a stricter rule for the reviewer: it may only report a defect if it ships a test that fails against the code in a sandbox. No failing test, no bug report.

The benchmark

I built FinCode-30: 30 small finance tasks (rounding, business-day calendars, payment splits). The hard part was not writing code from scratch, a cheap model does that fine. The hard part is code that already exists, passes its tests and is still wrong. So every task has:

  • public tests and hidden tests
  • three buggy variants: plausible one-line bugs that pass every public test and fail at least one hidden test
  • the clean reference, which no reviewer is allowed to break

On top of that there are 6 packages of three modules each, with one bug hidden in one module.

Results with an open-weights model

Held-out split (20 tasks, 60 buggy variants), prompts frozen before the run, the same open-weights model in every role:

Review mode Bugs fixed Correct code damaged
Free-text review 41/60 (68%) 0/20
Self-check (the model writes its own tests) 54/60 (90%) 0/20
Proof-gated review 57/60 (95%) 0/20

On the three-module packages: 17/18 for proof-gated review against 12/18 for free-text review. Cost was about 6 to 9 cents per target.

Where it did not help

With Meta's strongest hosted model as the reviewer, every condition fixed almost everything, and plain self-check was as good as proof-gated review and far cheaper. So the rule mostly lifts weaker models. What it adds for strong models is an audit trail: every reported defect comes with a test that fails, and each run keeps code, claims, tests and results, hashed with SHA-256 so it can be re-checked later.

One surprise: the reviewer's proven claims sometimes also failed on my own reference solutions. I read each of them against the spec; none contradicted it, and about half were real defects my references shared (for example dates with a trailing newline).

Limits

One model family, 30 tasks, finance only. I don't know yet how much of this carries over to larger codebases or messier domains.

Code, benchmark and full result tables: https://github.com/matrixagentsocial/matrix-globe

If you run agent code review in CI, I'd like to hear where this breaks.

This article was written with the help of AI (Claude) and checked against the published result tables before posting.

title: Two Agents, Two Definitions of 'Done': The Contract to Write Before You Wire Them Together
description:
The failure mode nobody writes about: two AI agents, both running, both "up" on every dashboard — and the job quietly not getting done.

On the November 11 episode of The Cognitive Revolution, Vijoy Pandey — SVP and GM of Outshift by Cisco, the incubation arm that has deployed multi-agent systems with Swisscom, ServiceNow, SoftServe, and Webex — described a gap that standard monitoring never shows. In Cisco's own five-agent deployments, accuracy fell from 99% with no misalignments between the agents to 16% with three. In one travel-booking test, the system was mostly up and connected while completing zero tasks. And in an analysis of public ChatDev sessions, Cisco reported semantic or cognitive-misalignment failures in 100% of the sessions it examined.

"Connectivity is not the same as cognition," Pandey told host Nathan Labenz. "What we need to move towards is shared cognition and shared reasoning."

His diagnosis: the industry measures whether agents are up and connected, while agents can be connected and still not understand each other. The value, he argued, is not in any one agent — "the value is actually in the handoff that's happening between these agents."

The failure isn't capability. It's vocabulary.

Most multi-agent advice focuses on architecture: which agent does what, who orchestrates, how they connect. The failure Pandey described is duller and more dangerous: two competent agents that mean different things by the same word.

At small-business scale, the version looks like this:

  • Your sales agent marks a job "done" when the customer accepts the quote.
  • Your invoicing agent considers the job "done" when payment clears.
  • Your sales agent calls someone a "customer" the moment they sign.
  • Your billing system calls them a "customer" only once an invoice exists.

Both definitions are defensible. Neither agent is broken. But the moment you wire automation across that seam — sales closes the job, invoicing starts billing — you have two different meanings of the trigger word routing real money. The handoff fires early, or late, or on the wrong population, and everything looks green while it happens.

Cisco's answer was to open-source three protocols, which Outshift describes as observe, align, and validate: Scope builds knowledge graphs on agent traces to find cognitive failures; Accord has agents agree on intent, scope, key terms, and the definition of "done" before work starts; Concord has agents negotiate an outcome every one can accept when they disagree.

You do not need to install any of that. You need the idea underneath it: the definitions get written down before the wiring, not after the failure.

The handoff contract: one page, 20 minutes

Before you connect any two agents — or an agent to a system it will trigger — write five fields. One page per seam; a three-agent setup has three seams, and each gets its own page.

1. Name the pair. "Sales agent → invoicing agent." Every contract covers exactly two systems. If a diagram is forming in your head, you're overcomplicating it — the contract is pairwise, not a hub.

2. List the words that cross the seam. Not every word — the load-bearing nouns, usually five or fewer: done, customer, paid, urgent, late. Pull the actual messages that will pass between the two systems and highlight the words both sides will act on.

3. Write each side's current definition. One line each, no editing, no fixing yet. Done (sales agent): quote accepted, kickoff email sent. Done (invoicing agent): invoice issued, payment reconciled. The differences are usually obvious the moment they're on paper — which is exactly why they need to be on paper.

4. Negotiate the shared definition. Where the two sides differ, write the one definition both will use — and make it checkable. "Done = quote accepted AND kickoff email sent AND invoice issued" is a definition an agent can test. "Done = the customer is taken care of" is a vibe. This is Accord's job shrunk to a paragraph.

5. Write the conflict rule. When a message arrives that doesn't fit the shared definitions, the receiving agent stops and asks a human. Never improvise a meaning. This is Concord's negotiation step shrunk to its SMB version: escalate, don't guess. The 99%-to-16% collapse came from misalignments that went uncorrected — the contract's job is to catch the collision while it's still a question, not a loss.

Then run one real past case through the seam before you turn the wiring on — the trickiest one from last month. If the two agents don't classify it identically against the contract, the contract isn't finished.

Where this fails (the honest list)

  • A contract fixes collisions, not competence. Perfect definitions make two agents agree; they don't make either one good. If the model writes a bad email, the contract just ensures both agents agree it was sent.
  • Sometimes the answer is one agent. If a single agent can do the whole job end to end, do that and skip the seam entirely. Contracts are for handoffs you actually need — don't create a second agent just to have something to wire.
  • The numbers are a warning, not a benchmark. The 99%-to-16% collapse and the 100% ChatDev figure come from Cisco's own deployments and its analysis of public sessions. They establish the failure mode exists, not your odds of hitting it.
  • Even the builders haven't finished. Pandey reported on the same episode that his own personal agent and his wife's — each carrying one identity across several models — still struggle to coordinate on their humans' behalf, down to booking a shared dinner. If the executive open-sourcing alignment protocols is still working on it, a one-page contract doesn't put you behind. It puts you ahead of most of the market.

Where to start

You can't write a handoff contract for agents you don't know you're running. Shadow usage means most small businesses already have two AI tools touching the same customers without anyone writing down what happens between them — one paid by the company, one installed by an employee, no shared definitions anywhere.

That's the first thing the AI Clarity Sprint maps: every AI touchpoint in your business — paid tools, AI features inside software you already own, and the employee shadow usage nobody approved — in two weeks, for one fixed fee ($1,495 CAD). You finish with the complete inventory, the seams worth writing contracts for, and a ranked plan for what to do first. The cheapest place to fix a misalignment is before the wiring. The second cheapest is the week you find the seam.

title: Your agent's "never" list should be a list of missing tools
description:
Most agent tutorials start general and keep adding tools. For a job you run every week, I've found it works better the other way around: write the one job on a card first, then let the card design the harness.

Six lines: input, steps, output, done when, risks, never. Each one turns into code:

  • Steps become tools, one per verb.
  • Done when becomes the eval suite.
  • Risks become hard caps: searches per turn, max steps, a token budget.
  • Never becomes the tools you leave out. No shell, no writes outside one folder. It's the cheapest safety feature there is.

The detail that mattered most for a research agent: models can produce a plausible URL that was never retrieved. So the harness keeps its own ledger of pages actually fetched (search snippets don't count) and refuses to save a brief citing anything else.

In my evals Haiku 5.5 passed 12 of 12 runs at about $0.43 per suite, Sonnet 5.5 passed 6 of 6 at about $2.54. Small sample, but enough to make Haiku my default for routine research.

If you'll only run a workflow twice, a general agent is probably the better use of your afternoon. If it repeats, the card gives you a cost ceiling and real tests.

The full step-by-step build (about 250 lines of Python with the Claude API, no framework) is here: Pick One Workflow, Then Build the Harness Around It

title: Can Agent Toolkit for AWS Make Coding Agents Better Engineers?
description:
Last year, I built a serverless AI chat application on AWS by hand. This year, I gave the same kind of spec to a coding agent. Twice.

Once on its own, and once with the Agent Toolkit for AWS installed. Same agent, same model, same prompt, same AWS account. The only thing I changed was the toolkit.

I wanted to answer one question:

Can AWS-specific tooling make a coding agent a better AWS engineer?

Here is what I built, how I tested it, and what actually changed (and what didn’t).

2025: Building My AI Chat Application

In 2025, I built a serverless AI chat application on AWS (I wrote about that build here).

At the time, I thought I was building a chatbot.

I wasn’t. I was building a distributed system.

The idea looked simple enough on paper.

A user sends a message. An AI model generates a response. The application displays the result.

But it introduced a different set of engineering challenges.

There were three requirements that shaped the architecture.

1. Real-Time Streaming

Most AI applications follow a frustrating pattern.

The model might be generating tokens immediately, but the user sees nothing until the response is ready.

I wanted users to see the response as it was being generated.

2. Access to External Knowledge

A regular chat application responds to what the model already knows.

I wanted mine to do more.

A planner could decide whether a tool was needed, trigger a Knowledge Base lookup, and pass the retrieved information to the model before generating the final response.

This introduced another layer to the application.

3. Fully Serverless

I didn't want infrastructure sitting idle.

If nobody used the application for a week, it would cost essentially nothing.

Eventually, the architecture settled into something like this:

Modern Agents Feel Different

Agentic coding tools are changing the way we develop software.

Traditionally, almost everything revolved around the engineer.

We made the decisions, wrote the code, connected the services, ran the application, and fixed the errors.

AI was there to assist us.

The first generation of AI coding assistants didn't fundamentally change how we worked.

They were better auto-complete engines.

Write a Lambda function.

They wrote a Lambda function.

But modern coding agents are different.

They can:

  • Read entire repositories.
  • Inspect files and understand existing code.
  • Execute commands.
  • Search documentation.
  • Identify errors and attempt to fix them.
  • Interact with cloud services.
  • Even deploy infrastructure.

The difference is quite significant.

They stopped suggesting and started acting. And once an agent can act inside your AWS account, two questions matter: does it know AWS well enough to do it right, and what stops it from doing something it shouldn't?

What Is the Agent Toolkit for AWS?

Before looking at the toolkit itself, it’s worth understanding why something like it needs to exist.

AWS contains hundreds of services, overlapping architectural patterns, and complex IAM relationships. Expecting either developers or coding agents to remember every service, best practice, and deployment nuance is unrealistic.

Most of the time, that’s fine. It stops being fine when you hit:

  1. Deployment errors
  2. Debugging challenges
  3. Troubleshooting complex service interactions

Modern agents can already write the code. What they struggle with is navigating the huge AWS ecosystem: picking the right API, the right permissions, and the right fix when something breaks. That’s exactly the gap the toolkit claims to fill.

What the Toolkit Claims to Do

The pitch is simple: help coding agents build on AWS effectively, with fewer errors and stronger security controls. AWS launched it in May 2026 as the successor to the MCP servers, plugins and skills that used to live in AWS Labs (product page).

It has three parts:

1. Skills

AWS-specific guides the agent can pull in while it works: best practices, architecture guidance, deployment steps and troubleshooting entries.

2. AWS MCP Server

A managed server that lets the agent work with AWS services directly and search up-to-date documentation while it builds. Instead of guessing from its training data, the agent can check what AWS currently recommends.

3. Plugins

Plugins bundle the MCP server configuration and a curated set of skills into one install, so we don't need to wire it up.

What I Tested

My study focuses on practical engineering outcomes. I looked at six areas:

  1. Deployment Success: Can the application be deployed successfully?
  2. Human Intervention: How often does it need my help?
  3. Architecture Decisions: Does the generated architecture make sense?
  4. Infrastructure Quality: Are AWS resources configured correctly?
  5. Security: Does it follow least-privilege principles?
  6. Cost and Efficiency: How much effort, time, and compute are required to reach a working solution?

What I'm Not Testing

  • Other agents and models. I use one agent and one pinned model, so results don't generalize.
  • General coding ability. This isn't a coding benchmark.
  • AWS versus other clouds.
  • Other regions. Everything runs in us-east-1.
  • The whole toolkit. I only test what affects building this chat app.

The Experiment

I wanted a fair test, so I changed exactly one thing.

My 2025 build is the story, not a scored condition. A and B are the comparison.

The question: does adding the Agent Toolkit for AWS change how well the same coding agent builds and deploys the same app?

The Assignment

Both runs got the same SPEC.md: a streaming AI chat backend on AWS, similar to the one I built by hand last year.

  • API Gateway WebSocket API
  • Lambda backend
  • Amazon Bedrock, streamed token by token
  • DynamoDB for session memory, so history survives reconnects
  • AWS CDK for deployment, with one command to deploy and one to destroy
  • Least-privilege IAM

The spec fixes the outside (how clients connect, how messages look, what tools to use). It leaves the inside open, so the agent picks its own architecture.

A run counts as successful if:

  • It deploys
  • Responses stream over WebSocket
  • Conversation history persists
  • Everything is defined in CDK

The Two Conditions

A, Agent Only: Claude Code with no Agent Toolkit for AWS installed.

Run A (no toolkit): the chat streams and remembers what I told it earlier.

B, Agent + Toolkit: The same Claude Code with the aws-core plugin installed (skills plus the AWS MCP Server).

Same model, same prompt, same AWS account, same region (us-east-1).

One note: my spec named the Bedrock model ID directly, which turned out to matter later.

Run B (with toolkit): same behavior, plus token counts for each message.

Setup Details

  • Coding agent: Claude Code, the same version and model for both runs
  • Toolkit: aws-core plugin, version 1.2.0
  • Model inside the app: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, through the US cross-region inference profile
  • Region and date: us-east-1, runs done at the end of October 2026

Keeping It Fair

The toolkit installs globally, not per project. If I’d installed it first, A would have quietly used B’s skills. So I ran A before installing the plugin, then installed it for B. Each run started in a fresh folder containing only SPEC.md, and the stack was destroyed and checked before the next run.

The cost of this setup: A ran before B, so time of day and model changes weren't balanced.

The Rules

  • Identical prompt for every run
  • I only helped when stuck. Typing “continue” or pasting an error counts as a soft intervention; anything that adds new information counts as a hard one. I logged everything in each run’s RESULT.md.
  • This is a small field test, not a benchmark, so I show every run.

How I Scored It

By checking, not by feel:

  • Manual WebSocket tests: tokens stream, history survives a reconnect
  • Minutes to a working result
  • Interventions
  • Usage from the agent's report
  • IAM wildcard count

One more source of evidence: I asked B to explain what the toolkit contributed (TOOLKIT_USAGE.md). That’s the agent grading itself, so I checked every claim against run A and the transcript. Both files are linked at the end.

Results

The outcome was the same. The path was not.

At first glance, the results looked almost identical. Both runs produced a working application that deployed, streamed responses, and remembered the conversation.

The time didn’t separate them either. A took 21 minutes and B took 20. A one-minute gap is noise, not a win, so I’m not counting it as one.

Where the runs did differ was effort. B used about 30k tokens against A’s 45k. B needed only soft interventions, while A needed one hard one, where I had to give it information it couldn’t work out from the error messages alone.

The runtime difference has a simple explanation. B’s CDK skill told it to run cdk synth --strict before deploying, which surfaced a deprecation warning for nodejs20.x, so B moved to nodejs22.x. A stayed on nodejs20.x.

I expected a clear winner, and I didn’t get one. Even the problems were the same: both runs hit the same Bedrock model error caused by my spec, and both had to fix cross-region IAM permissions.

The Same Error, Two Different Paths

My spec named the model directly: anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0. Bedrock rejected it with an “on-demand throughput isn’t supported” error. This model has to be called through an inference profile, so the fix is the profile ID: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0.

That fix caused the second problem. The us. profile routes requests across us-east-1, us-east-2 and us-west-2, so an IAM policy scoped only to us-east-1 starts failing as soon as a request lands in another region. Both runs had to allow the foundation model ARNs in all three regions, plus the inference profile ARN.

A worked from the error messages. It read what AWS was telling it, made its own API calls, and pieced the answer together.

B had loaded two skills before writing any code: aws-core:aws-cdk and aws-core:amazon-bedrock. The Bedrock skill had a troubleshooting entry for exactly this error: list the inference profiles and use the profile ID. It also explained that us. profiles route across regions, which pointed straight at the IAM fix.

Even then, B mostly made the AWS call itself rather than going through the MCP server. The skills didn't replace the agent's work. They told it which calls to make and what to look for.

The skill also flagged a problem neither run hit in testing. According to B’s notes, it marked a missing maxTokens as a critical warning: leave it out and Claude reserves its full output limit against your quota, which the skill calls the #1 cause of unexpected ThrottlingException. B set it to 1024. A happened to set 4096, so it was fine here, but nothing told it why that matters.

Going in, I expected the toolkit to help the agent write better code. That isn't what happened. The generated code worked in both conditions, and most of the problems weren't coding problems at all. They were deployment problems: permissions, Bedrock configuration, and service setup.

The toolkit behaved less like a code assistant and more like an AWS specialist sitting next to the agent.

The difference wasn’t intelligence. The difference was context.

Production Readiness Checklist

At this point, both implementations looked remarkably similar. Both applications deployed successfully, streamed responses, preserved conversation history, and passed most of the tests I had originally defined. If I stopped here, the conclusion would be simple: both approaches work.

But that's not enough. The hardest problems rarely appear during deployment. They appear weeks later, real users connect; conversations grow longer, costs increase, and error logs start filling up. I had already learned many of these lessons the hard way while building a similar application in 2025.

So I decided to run one more test.

Neither a deployment test nor a functionality test.

A production readiness test.

I took the problems I had encountered in my earlier implementation and turned them into another set of engineering checks.

I wanted to look beyond whether the application worked and understand how well it was engineered.

I split the checks into two groups: implementation details (did it make good choices in code and infrastructure?) and operational concerns (would it survive real traffic?).

Check A: Agent only B: Agent + Toolkit Notes
Implementation details
Retry on Bedrock failures Fail Pass A: SDK defaults only. B: retryMode: "adaptive" with maxAttempts set.
Bedrock API choice Partial Pass A: InvokeModelWithResponseStream with model-specific parsing. B: ConverseStream, model-agnostic events.
Sliding window for history Fail Pass A: loads the oldest 50 messages (stale context). B: keeps the newest with slice(-MAX_HISTORY).
JSON and error handling Partial Pass A: generic handler that leaks err.message. B: try/catch with a clean 400 response.
DynamoDB grants per function Partial Pass A: grantReadWriteData on all 3 functions. B: write-only for connect/disconnect, read/write only where needed.
Bedrock IAM scoped to model ARNs Pass Pass Both: inference profile plus the 3 regional model ARNs. No bedrock:*.
Explicit maxTokens Pass Pass A: 4096. B: 1024.
Operational concerns
Lambda timeout vs API Gateway Fail Fail Both: 120s Lambda timeout against the 29s API Gateway integration limit.
GoneException handling Fail Fail Neither stops streaming when the client disconnects mid-response.
DynamoDB TTL Fail Fail Old sessions are never cleaned up.
WebSocket reconnect Fail Fail Neither frontend reconnects automatically.
Authentication Fail Fail Anyone with the URL can connect. My spec did not ask for it either, so this one is on me too.
Total (12 checks) 2 pass, 3 partial, 7 fail 7 pass, 5 fail B ahead on 5 checks, all implementation details.

B came out ahead on 5 of the 12 checks, all of them implementation details. On the 5 operational checks, the runs were identical: both failed every one.

IAM wildcards are in the results table above: neither run used a wildcard action. One small detail went A’s way, though. B kept one CDK-generated wildcard resource on its log-retention helper, while A removed it by switching to explicit LogGroup constructs.

Key Takeaways

  • A had one real bug: once a conversation passes 50 messages, the model gets the oldest history instead of the newest. Short tests never show it.
  • B used a third fewer tokens and needed only soft interventions. Time was nearly the same.
  • B’s edge came from the skills: the inference profile fix, the Converse API, adaptive retries and tighter DynamoDB grants all trace back to them.
  • On the operational checks, both runs missed the same things: timeout alignment, GoneException, DynamoDB TTL, reconnect logic and authentication. These are the problems we usually learn by running software under real traffic.
  • Limits: one run each, an agent-assisted audit, and checks partly chosen after seeing the code. Some differences may be run-to-run variation.

Try It Yourself

If you want to repeat this, or just use what B got right in your own project, here is the short version.

1. Install the toolkit in Claude Code 

/plugin marketplace add aws/agent-toolkit-for-aws
/plugin install aws-core@agent-toolkit-for-aws
/reload-plugins

If you are running a comparison like mine, install it after your baseline run. It installs globally, so every project on your machine picks up the skills. Setup for other agents like Codex and Kiro is in the official docs.

2. Use the inference profile, and scope IAM to every region it routes to 

const profileId = "us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0";
const modelId = "anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0";

sendMessageFn.addToRolePolicy(new iam.PolicyStatement({
  actions: ["bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"],
  resources: [
    `arn:aws:bedrock:${this.region}:${this.account}:inference-profile/${profileId}`,
    ...["us-east-1", "us-east-2", "us-west-2"].map(
      (r) => `arn:aws:bedrock:${r}::foundation-model/${modelId}`
    ),
  ],
}));

3. Stream with ConverseStream, adaptive retries and an explicit maxTokens 

import { BedrockRuntimeClient, ConverseStreamCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime";

const bedrock = new BedrockRuntimeClient({
  retryMode: "adaptive",
  maxAttempts: 3,
});

const response = await bedrock.send(new ConverseStreamCommand({
  modelId: process.env.MODEL_ID, // the us. inference profile
  messages: history,
  inferenceConfig: { maxTokens: 1024 },
}));

for await (const event of response.stream) {
  const text = event.contentBlockDelta?.delta?.text;
  if (text) await send(connectionId, { type: "chunk", text });
}

4. Load the newest history, not the oldest

A’s bug is a classic one. A DynamoDB Query returns items in ascending sort-key order, so Limit: 50 gives you the first 50 messages ever sent. Read newest first, then flip the order back for the model:

const { Items } = await ddb.send(new QueryCommand({
  TableName: process.env.MESSAGES_TABLE,
  KeyConditionExpression: "sessionId = :s",
  ExpressionAttributeValues: { ":s": sessionId },
  ScanIndexForward: false, // newest first
  Limit: 50,
}));
const history = Items.reverse(); // oldest to newest again

5. Give each function only what it needs 

connectionsTable.grantWriteData(connectFn);
connectionsTable.grantWriteData(disconnectFn);
connectionsTable.grantReadData(sendMessageFn);
conversationsTable.grantReadWriteData(sendMessageFn);

6. Add what neither run did

Both runs missed these, so add them yourself:

// Stop streaming when the client has left
try {
  await apigw.send(new PostToConnectionCommand({ ConnectionId: connectionId, Data: payload }));
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name === "GoneException") clientGone = true; // stop the loop
  else throw err;
}

// CDK: expire old sessions automatically
const conversationsTable = new dynamodb.Table(this, "ConversationsTable", {
  partitionKey: { name: "sessionId", type: dynamodb.AttributeType.STRING },
  sortKey: { name: "timestamp", type: dynamodb.AttributeType.NUMBER },
  timeToLiveAttribute: "expiresAt",
});
  • Line up the Lambda timeout with the 29-second API Gateway integration limit.
  • Add a Lambda authorizer on the $connect route.
  • Reconnect with backoff in the frontend, and reuse the same session ID.

Bottom Line

I started with one question: can a modern coding agent build the same system end-to-end, and does AWS-native tooling change the outcome?

Both runs built a working app. The outcome wasn’t the difference. The path was. B read its answers from skills, and A worked them out from error messages.

On implementation details, B came out ahead on 5 of my 12 checks. On the problems you only learn by operating a system, they were identical.

The toolkit changed the defaults the agent picked in the areas its skills cover. It didn’t touch what you only learn by running the system. That part is still on us.

What I keep coming back to:

Building software is rarely about knowing the answer. It’s about finding the right answer before the mistake becomes a lesson.

Thanks to Krishnendu Sukumar for his help with this experiment and article.

References

  • GitHub repository

  • TOOLKIT_USAGE.md

  • Results - A
  • Agent Toolkit for AWS (product page)
  • Agent Toolkit for AWS plugins (docs)

title: Graphicle: a code graph and project memory for coding agents
description:
Graphicle

Agent memory goes stale the moment the code it describes changes. Graphicle is one Rust program that gives a coding agent a code graph and project memory together, over MCP. It maps the repository, keeps docs, reviewed decisions and past agent sessions, and returns cited excerpts with exact files and lines. The useful part is the link between the two: a reviewed decision is pinned to the function it describes, and once that function changes, Graphicle withholds the decision instead of serving it as current. It runs locally, with no account and no API key. Created 14 October, it is already at v0.1.18, with 598 stars on GitHub.

What you get

  • A code graph and project memory in one program, served to a coding agent over MCP
  • Cited excerpts with exact files and lines, so the agent quotes the repo instead of recalling it
  • Reviewed decisions pinned to the function they describe, withheld the moment that function changes
  • Local only, no account and no API key, Apache-2.0, latest release v0.1.18

Agent memory that cannot tell when the code changed is a liability, not a feature. Pin the decision to the function, and withhold it when the function moves.

Repo: https://github.com/Graphicle-AI/graphicle

Quick poll

What would you use Graphicle for first?

  • Giving my coding agent a code graph to search
  • Pinning reviewed decisions to the code they describe
  • Replacing stale agent memory with repo-grounded memory
  • Running it locally on a real repo first

Vote in the comments.

If you found Graphicle interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: How Claude’s Agent Memory Works
description:
On November 6, Anthropic published a technical brief outlining its native memory architecture for Claude Agents. The design splits long-term memory into four distinct tiers, paired with an asynchronous background process called dreaming. Rather than focusing purely on maximizing information retention, the system is optimized to decide what information to discard, validate, and prioritize. A well-known Pokémon experiment included in the document illustrates this core principle: a model that wrote 413 separate memory files only collected 1 in-game badge, while another model that maintained just 9 carefully curated files earned 4 badges. This article breaks down the layered memory stack, the mechanics of dreaming, supporting experimental metrics, unresolved limitations, and practical implications for agent developers.

1. The Four-Layer Memory Stack

Anthropic organizes agent memory along two axes: persistence and information density. The four layers form a sequential processing pipeline, where raw conversation data flows upward through extraction, synthesis, and promotion. Higher layers contain sparser, higher-value records that load rapidly at the start of a new session.

Layer Content Origin
Layer 1: Raw Conversation Logs Full, unmodified record of dialogue, observations, actions and tool returns Captured live during agent execution, no transformation
Layer 2: Memory Notes Extracted observations, recurring patterns, constraints, behavioural rules and verified facts Derived from raw logs during active interaction and offline dreaming
Layer 3: Knowledge Wiki Cross-session synthesized knowledge, structured as interconnected wiki-style entries Aggregated and merged from validated memory notes
Layer 4: Resident Context High-priority wiki entries and notes automatically injected at the start of each new conversation Selected from the knowledge wiki based on access frequency and relevance

The stack operates as a one-way refinement workflow. Raw logs act as immutable source material. Notes are intermediate artifacts. The wiki represents consolidated knowledge. Resident context is the small, fast subset loaded automatically for every new turn.

A critical architectural rule governs the whole system: original conversation logs are never altered. All edits, corrections and revisions produce new copies of notes and wiki entries. Outdated records can simply be discarded. This immutability gives the memory system a built-in undo capability. The design draws academic inspiration from sleep-time compute research from Letta and UC Berkeley, framing offline processing as a mechanism for grounding learned facts against historical interaction traces.

2. Active-Time Memory as Prediction

Memory notes are often misread as simple conversation summaries. Anthropic frames them differently: every stored note is a predictive claim about future utility. Writing a rule means predicting that this pattern will reappear in later tasks. Saving a verified fact means predicting that the agent will rely on it repeatedly without re-deriving the conclusion. This predictive nature introduces inherent risk. If the prediction is wrong, the stored note becomes stale and may mislead subsequent sessions.

This framing yields a clear principle: memory quality is not measured by how much information it stores, but by how accurately it anticipates future requirements. A note stating “the user prefers concise answers” is a high-value prediction. A note recording “there are three enemies visible on screen right now” is low-value, because the environment state will be available directly in the next turn.

Anthropic explicitly scopes this memory system. It does not cover attention weighting, single-turn in-context learning, or run-time context compression. It exclusively refers to persistent, cross-session records stored as readable text artifacts.

3. The Pokémon Experiment: 413 Files versus 9 Files

Anthropic tested memory selection behaviour using a controlled Pokémon environment. Each agent received a writable memory directory and decided independently what to persist. The contrast between the two test configurations demonstrates the core thesis of the memory design.

  • Claude Sonnet 3.7 created 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned only one badge. Its strategy assumed nearly every state detail might become useful. It logged every battle outcome, item and NPC state. The rapidly expanding archive created retrieval overhead. After roughly 10,000 steps, the agent created a fourth top-level memory folder and spent most of its runtime reading old records instead of progressing through the game.
  • Claude Fable 5 maintained only 9 files and 2 folders, plus a global global.md index. It collected four badges. Fable’s strategy ignored transient, observable state such as gold count, position and current health. Those values could be read directly from the interface at any time. Instead, it stored latent knowledge: strategy notes, validated rules, and lessons learned from failed attempts. The global file tracked high-level objectives; location files stored route plans; gameplay files recorded refined tactics from repeated failures.

The experiment’s conclusion is foundational: memory capacity is defined by filtering decisions, not storage volume. Retention is valuable only when it captures information that cannot be reliably observed at the moment of need.

4. Steering Judgement, Not Hard Scripted Rules

Many engineering teams building memory systems begin with rigid filter rules such as “only record failures” or “only store user preferences”. Anthropic’s internal tests show this approach works inconsistently, and performance varies sharply by model capability tier.

When Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 were given a hard rule to record only failures, their overall memory utility declined. Stronger models can already distinguish useful signals from noise. Overly restrictive rules strip away valid insights the model would otherwise identify. The recommended pattern is to tell the model the purpose of memory, rather than dictating exactly what to write.

The opposite behaviour appears on weaker models. Sonnet 4.6 rarely consults its own memory or validates prior mistakes without explicit prompting. Adding a simple steering instruction to read memory and test hypotheses before responding nearly doubled its benchmark scores. Sonnet 5, by contrast, performs this validation autonomously in most cases.

This creates a practical product pattern: the same memory stack acts as an amplifier for capable models, while it functions primarily as a noise collector for weaker ones. Complex memory pipelines cannot compensate for limited native reasoning ability.

5. What the Dreaming Process Executes

Dreaming is the official term for the asynchronous offline batch job that runs when the agent is not actively handling user requests. It is not a generative hallucination step. Every dreaming run executes three fixed operations:

  1. Extract new candidate notes from recent interactions, including stable user preferences, recurring behavioural patterns, recorded errors and confirmed corrections.
  2. Merge new notes into the knowledge wiki, deduplicate redundant records, replace outdated entries and reconcile conflicting claims.
  3. Promote the most frequently accessed and high-impact wiki entries into resident context, so they load automatically for the next session without separate retrieval calls.

Several engineering constraints shape dreaming execution. A single job can process between 1 and 100 conversation histories. Runtime ranges from minutes to hours, scaling with the volume of source logs. The input log corpus remains untouched; the output is a fresh set of notes and wiki artifacts. Developers can use high-level instructions to guide dreaming behaviour, but the process operates at the aggregate synthesis level and does not support fine-grained line-by-line editing of memory records.

The Pokémon example of a navigation loop illustrates dreaming’s grounding function. One agent repeatedly failed to navigate out of a cave. During active runs, it consistently misrecorded the exit direction. When dreaming triggered, the model cross-referenced its notes against immutable raw conversation logs. It detected the mismatch between written memory and actual action traces, revised the flawed note, and successfully navigated the route in subsequent attempts. This shows raw logs serve as the ground truth anchor for memory correction. Without the immutable log layer, dreaming can only reproduce the model’s prior misconceptions.

6. Measured Gains: From 13% to 48%, and the Remaining 52%

Anthropic published long-term wiki benchmark results using a corpus of roughly 35,000 documents and 4.2 billion tokens of technical documentation. The test set required cross-document synthesis.

  • Baseline accuracy, using only the final state of the wiki without offline dreaming: 13%
  • After 128 dreaming cycles: accuracy rose to 48%
  • Adding retrieval-augmented access to the raw document corpus lifted accuracy to 61%
  • When constrained to a 2,000-token context budget, the combined dreaming plus retrieval setup delivered 53% accuracy

The 48% figure marks a nearly fourfold improvement over the baseline, confirming that offline consolidation accumulates usable knowledge. At the same time, it highlights the hard upper bound: 52% of the evaluation questions still failed even after 128 consolidation passes.

This gap reveals a key behavioural trait of dreaming. It corrects mistakes that leave clear feedback traces. It is far less effective for domains with delayed or ambiguous outcomes. In coding, testing and gaming, failure signals appear immediately. In business judgement or market forecasting, bad decisions may only become visible much later, if at all. Those latent errors can persist in the wiki indefinitely.

Separate benchmark gains were observed on CL-Bench. Opus 5.5 improved from 0.655 to 0.838, and Sonnet 4.6 moved from 0.330 to 0.364 after the introduction of the dreaming consolidation workflow.

7. Known Limitations of the Design

Anthropic’s documentation lists four major limitations, ordered by impact severity.

First, restricted availability. Dreaming is currently limited to Claude Managed Agents research preview. It requires a dedicated beta HTTP header. Teams working with standard API integrations or third-party agent frameworks cannot access this native offline pipeline today.

Second, saturation of returns. 48% represents the measured endpoint after 128 cycles. Further repeated dreaming brings diminishing marginal gains. Higher reliability requires cleaner source traces rather than additional consolidation passes.

Third, non-determinism. Memory updates are non-deterministic. Identical queries may receive different answers at different times, as the set of active notes and wiki entries evolves. This creates compliance challenges for workloads requiring stable, repeatable outputs.

Fourth, rising audit overhead. The immutability guarantee means every dreaming pass generates new storage artifacts. Frequent dreaming creates a growing version history of memory snapshots. Saved token cost is partially traded for increased human review labour.

8. Core Decision Rules for Memory Engineering

The technical summary consolidates three foundational judgements for memory system design.

  1. The core of memory design is selective forgetting. The Pokémon experiment demonstrates that retention volume is not correlated with performance.
  2. Dreaming is grounded validation, not autonomous reasoning. It relies on immutable raw logs as ground truth. Without source logs, dreaming merely rehashes prior model assumptions.
  3. Memory is an amplifier for model capability. Strong base models gain substantial value from structured memory; weaker models see limited uplift and accumulate noise.

These rules shift the implementation focus away from unlimited storage and toward filtering, grounding, and capability matching.

9. Implications for Agent Builders

For teams building production agents, this architecture delivers three actionable design principles.

First, implement layered storage. Do not merge all records into a single flat memory table. Separate immutable logs, volatile notes, synthesized wiki knowledge, and hot resident context. Tiered storage reduces search overhead and isolates risk. Unified routing and observability become simpler when memory, tool calls and model inference are managed through a consistent control plane, and 4sapi delivers this gateway abstraction for mixed-model agent stacks.

Second, prioritize forgetting strategies before retention strategies. For every candidate memory record, evaluate whether the information can be read directly from the environment or the current prompt on the next turn. If it is observable on demand, persistent storage is usually unnecessary.

Third, prefer steering instructions over rigid filter scripts. Early-stage guardrails can guide behaviour, but hard filters such as “only record failures” degrade performance on capable models. Let the model judge what to keep, while clearly stating the purpose of memory.

Developers should also budget for cost growth. Offline dreaming pipelines scale cost with conversation history length and processing frequency. It is economical to validate consolidation workflows on small traffic segments before rolling out frequent background jobs broadly. The same applies to audit processes; every generation of memory artifacts adds to review workloads.

Closing

Anthropic’s four-layer memory stack and dreaming process represent a distinct departure from simple vector database retrieval designs. The system treats memory as a predictive asset, validated periodically against immutable interaction logs. The Pokémon experiment and long-term wiki benchmarks prove that selective forgetting is as important as remembering for agent performance. Even so, the workflow carries practical constraints: limited preview access, diminishing returns, non-determinism and audit burden must all be weighed before adoption. The pattern is most suitable for capable foundation models that can interpret steering guidance and self-filter useful knowledge.
